Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 76, verse 1:

﴿Has there come upon man a period of time when he was not a thing worth mentioning?﴾

It is an interrogative of affirmation (istifham taqriri). The interrogative (istifham) is one of the types of address (khitab). Here it is directed at no specific person, and it is used to establish the matter being affirmed, by way of indirect expression (kinaya), because the interrogative is a request for understanding (talab al-fahm), while affirmation (taqrir) requires that knowledge be obtained of what is being affirmed. This is an indication that God deserves that man acknowledge His oneness in lordship (al-wahdaniyya fi al-rububiyya), refuting the polytheism of the polytheists.

The placing of this interrogative at the beginning serves to arouse curiosity (tashwiq) about what follows in the speech.

Thus the clause ﴿Has there come upon man﴾ is a preliminary and introduction (tamhid wa tawti'a) to the clause that follows it, which is ﴿Indeed, We created man from a drop of mingled fluid﴾ [al-Insan: 2], and so on.

[p. 372]

The particle (هل, hal) is a letter that conveys the sense of interrogation and of confirmation (tahqiq). A group of scholars said: the original function of (hal) in interrogation is like that of (qad) in declarative statements. Because (hal) is used exclusively with interrogation, the omission of the interrogative particle along with it became common in speech, so that it carried the meaning of (qad). It was restricted to interrogation, so it does not occur in declarative statements. Whatever uses apply to interrogation with other particles also apply to interrogation with (hal). The explanation of this was already given at His words, exalted is He, ﴿Do they await anything but that God should come to them in canopies of cloud?﴾ [al-Baqara: 210], in Surat al-Baqara.

You have learned that when the interrogative is understood in the sense of affirmation, this meaning is achieved.

The meaning is: Does every existing human being acknowledge that he was non-existent for a long time, and was not a thing that is mentioned, that is, he was not named, and no one speaks of him by his own identity? Though he may be mentioned in general terms, as in the saying of people: "The non-existent depends for its existence on an agent," and the saying of the one who endows property: "I have endowed (habastu) for my descendants," and similar expressions. For that is not a mention of a specific individual, but a judgment about a matter whose existence is presumed. Human beings cannot but acknowledge this, so it suffices to direct this affirmation to every hearer.

The definite article in (al-insan, "the human being") is for comprehensiveness (istighraq), like His words, ﴿Indeed, man is in loss﴾ [al-'Asr: 2], ﴿except those who believe﴾ [al-'Asr: 3], and so on. That is, has there come upon every human being a period in which he was non-existent?

Al-dahr: a long span of time, or the time coextensive with the existence of the worldly world.

Al-hin: an indefinite measure of time, applied to an hour and to more than that. It has been said that the longest period to which (hin) is applied is forty years, but I do not think so.

The clause ﴿he was not a thing worth mentioning﴾ may be a qualifier (na't) of (hin), with an implied resumptive pronoun (damir rabit) attached to an omitted element, the indication being that the returning pronoun is governed by the adverbial preposition (harf al-zarfiyya), which is omitted together with its governor, as in His words, ﴿and fear a day when no soul will avail another soul anything﴾ [al-Baqara: 48]. The implied meaning there is: no soul will avail another soul anything in it. Here the implied meaning is: man was not in it a thing worth mentioning, that is, he was non-existent in a time that had passed.

The clause may also be a circumstantial clause (hal) of (al-insan), with the returning pronoun omitted as in its omission in the qualifier construction.

[p. 373]

Al-shay' (thing): a name for the existent.

Al-madhkur (worth mentioning): the specific entity that is such that it can be mentioned, that is, that is referred to by its particular identity and reported about through reports and states. Its word, which indicates it, is connected to actions.

As for the non-existent, it is not mentioned, because it has no specific identity, so it is mentioned only by its general title, as already stated above. This is not what is meant by "mention" here.

For this reason we take (madhkur) as a qualifier of (shay'an), by which the restriction of (shay'an) is intended, that is, a specific thing: the existent, expressed by its definite name.

[Page 374 of the source]

This is an explanatory resumptive clause (*isti'naf bayani*), following on from the statement implied by ﴿Has there come upon man a period of time when he was not a thing worth mentioning?﴾ (76:1), because of the sense of anticipation it creates.

The statement necessarily requires acknowledgement of this, since it is known necessarily. The hearer is therefore eager for what follows this statement, so it is said to him that God created him after he had been non-existent. He brought into existence a drop (*nutfah*) that had been non-existent, then brought forth from it a human being. Thus the connection of creation to the human being after his non-existence is established.

The emphasis of the speech with the particle *inna* ("indeed") is to treat the polytheists as if they were those who deny that God created man, because they did not act in accordance with what knowledge requires, as they worshipped idols that they had not created.

The word "*al-insan*" (man) is used in the same sense as in ﴿Has there come upon man﴾ (76:1), that is, the whole species of mankind.

Incorporated into this is the manner in which man was created from the drop of procreation, because in that manner there are subtleties of divine knowledge, power and wisdom.

The meaning of *nutfah* has already been discussed in Surah al-Qiyamah.

*Amshaj* (mingled) is derived from *mashj*, which means mixing; that is, a mingled drop. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Glory be to Him who created all the pairs from what the earth grows, and from themselves, and from what they do not know﴾ (36:36). This explains the meaning of mixing referred to here.

The form *amshaj* apparently has the form of a plural, and al-Farra', Ibn al-Sikkit and al-Mubarrad understood it thus. It is therefore either the plural of *mishj* (with a kasra and sukun, on the pattern of *'adl*), meaning *mamshuj*, i.e. mixed, like *dhibh*, and this is what is restricted to in *al-Lisan* and *al-Qamus*; or the plural of *mashaj* (with two fathas), like *sabab* and *asbab*; or the plural of *mashij* (with fatha then kasra), like *katif* and *akutaf*.

The correct view is that of the author of *al-Kashshaf* (al-Zamakhshari): that *amshaj* is a singular, like the expressions *burmat a'shar* (a cooking pot of tens) and *burd akyash* (a garment of ... [the word is] *akyash*, which denotes a cloth that has been re-spun twice). He said: "It is not correct that *amshaj* should be the plural of *mashij*; rather, both (*mashij* and *amshaj*) are equal in being singular." End of quotation. Some writers said that he contradicted the words of Sibawayh. Al-Baydawi alluded to this, but I think that he did not see Sibawayh's words as explicitly preventing *amshaj* from being a singular, since Sibawayh affirmed the singular in the word *an'am*; and al-Zamakhshari is well known for his strict adherence to Sibawayh.

If *amshaj* in this verse is a singular, it has the form of a plural, as in *al-Kashshaf*. Then describing the drop as *amshaj* requires no interpretation. If it is a plural, as the words of al-Farra', Ibn al-Sikkit and al-Mubarrad indicate, then the description of the drop with it is in consideration of the various parts of differing properties contained in the drop, so that each part of the drop becomes a limb. Thus the drop is described with a plural form of the noun for emphasis, meaning extremely mixed.

Some of these mixtures are chemical plant or earthly components, and some are the elements of the powers of life.

The clause ﴿We try him﴾ (*nabtalihi*) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*) relating to man, and it is a future-oriented circumstantial clause (*hal muqaddarah*), meaning: intending to try him in the future, that is, after he reaches the stage of reason and moral responsibility. This circumstantial clause is like their saying: "I passed by a man with a falcon, hunting with it tomorrow."

This circumstantial clause has come as an interposition between the clause ﴿We created﴾ (*khalaqna*) and ﴿so We made him hearing and seeing﴾ (76:2), because trial, that is, moral responsibility by which obedience or disobedience to it is manifested, occurs only after his guidance to the path of good. The apparent order would have been for *nabtalihi* to come after the clause ﴿Indeed We guided him to the way﴾ (76:3). However, it was placed first for emphasis on this trial, which is the cause of happiness and misery.

[Page 375 of the source]

The clause ﴿Indeed We guided him to the way﴾ (76:3) has been brought as an explanation of the clause *nabtalihi*, as a variation in the arrangement of speech.

The real meaning of trial (*ibtila'*) is testing in order to know the state of a thing. Here it is a metonymy (*kinayah*) for imposing moral responsibility for a great matter, because a great matter reveals the variation among those charged with it in fulfilling its establishment.

From his creation from a drop it follows that He made him hearing and seeing. This refers to the senses God created for him, which were the basis of his thinking and reflection. For this reason he is described as "hearing, seeing" in the intensive form, and it was not said "so We made him a hearer, a seer," because man's hearing and sight are more comprehensive in apprehension and discrimination of what is heard and seen than the hearing and sight of animals. Through hearing he receives the laws and the call of the messengers, and through sight he looks into the evidences of God's existence and His wondrous creation.

This is a transition (*takhallus*) to that by which God distinguished man: His making him disposed to moral responsibility and to following the laws. This is the distinctive feature of man by which his civilisation was founded and his communities were organised. For this reason this clause is followed by His saying ﴿Indeed We guided him to the way﴾ (76:3), and the verses that follow.

**Ibn 'Ashur, *al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir*, on Surah 76, verse 3:**

﴿Indeed, We guided him to the way, either grateful or ungrateful.﴾

This is an explanatory resumption (*istiʾnaf bayani*), which explains what follows from the clause "We will test him" (*nabtalihi*) and elaborates the clause "﴿So We made him hearing and seeing﴾" (al-Insan: 2). It also transitions to the threat against disbelief and the promise for gratitude.

The guidance to the way (*hidayat al-sabil*) is a metaphor (*tamthil*) for the state of the one who gives guidance. *Al-sabil* means the straight road leading to what is beneficial, through the messengers, to correct beliefs and righteous deeds, which are the cause of his success in everlasting bliss. This is like the state of one who points a traveller to the road that leads to his destination.

This metaphor resolves into comparisons between the parts of the composite state being compared and the parts of the state used for comparison. God, exalted is He, is like the guide. The human being resembles the traveller who is bewildered on the road. The deeds of religion resemble the road. The success of one who follows God's guidance resembles arriving at the desired place.

In this address there is an indication that God guided humankind to the truth, and that some people brought upon themselves the misguidance of belief and the corruptions of deeds. Whoever clears himself of that is the grateful one, and whoever does not is the ungrateful one. This is a division according to the condition of people at the beginning of the mission. Then there appeared those who mixed a righteous deed with an evil one.

The emphasis of the statement with *inna* (indeed) is to refute the polytheists who claim that what the Qur'an calls them to is false.

[p. 376]

The phrase "*shakiran wa-immā kafuran*" (﴿either grateful or ungrateful﴾) comprises two circumstantial clauses (*hal*) referring to the pronoun of the third person in *hadaynahu*, which refers to *al-insan* (the human being).

*Imma* is a particle of distinction (*harf tafsil*). It is a simple particle according to the majority. Sibawayh said it is composed of the conditional particle *in* and the negative particle *ma*. By composition, *in* became detached from the conditional sense just as *ma* became detached from negation, so that the whole of *imma* became a particle of distinction, with no governing effect on the noun following it, and it does not prevent the governing word preceding it from governing its complement following it. In this respect it is like the definite article *al-*. Some grammarians construed the second *imma* as a conjunctive particle (*harf ʿatf*), which is an arbitrary judgement, since they made the second one conjunctive while it is the sister of the first. Rather, the conjunctive particle is only *wa* (and), and *imma* is inserted between the noun and its complement, as in the verse of Ta'abbata Sharran:

*They are two strands: either captivity and a favour,*
*or blood, and death is more fitting for the free man.*

The two nouns after *imma* in both places of the verse are in the genitive by annexation (*idafa*), and for this reason the nun has been dropped from *khuttatā* in his words *humā khuttatā*, which is the more eloquent form, as occurs in this verse.

Ibn Jinni said: As for the one who puts *isar* in the genitive, he has dropped the nun for annexation and did not consider *imma* as a separator between the annexing and the annexed. On this basis you say: *humā immā ghulāmā Zaydin wa-immā ʿAmrin*. Better than this is that you say: *humā khuttatā isarin wa-minnatin wa-immā khuttatā damin*. Then he said: As for the nominative, it is the usual path, and its apparent basis is that it is in the dialect of those who drop the nun for reasons other than annexation, for this has been reported, etc.

The implication of his statement is that the verse was transmitted with both readings, the genitive and the nominative. Close to this is the statement of al-Marzuqi, who added: The dropping of the nun when *isar* is in the nominative is an extension of the noun, as if he extended *khuttatā* by its substitute, which is his saying: *immā isarun*, etc.

The meaning is: We guided him to the way while his situation was undetermined between one of these two descriptions:

[p. 377]

the description of the grateful and the description of the ungrateful. One of the two descriptions, in the alternative, is concomitant with the state of his being guided to the way, and this concomitance is conventional, i.e., immediately following the conveyance and reflection. If he takes up the guidance, he is grateful; if he turns away, he is ungrateful. This is like one who does not follow the guidance of the one who points him to the road, and so takes a path on which he meets wild beasts or thieves. With this the metaphor that is in his saying ﴿Indeed, We guided him to the way﴾ is complete.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 76, verse 4:

﴿Indeed, We have prepared for the disbelievers chains and shackles and a blazing Fire.﴾

The aim is to move on to the recompense of the two groups, the grateful and the ungrateful.

The sentence is resumed (isti'naf) in the explanatory mode (istinaf bayani), because His saying (﴿Either grateful or ungrateful﴾ [al-Insan: 3]) arouses the listeners' anticipation to know the consequences of these two states between which one's condition wavers. So it begins with the recompense of the disbeliever, since mention of him is nearer.

He emphasized the report of the threat with the particle of emphasis (harf al-ta'kid) in order to instil fear in them, for when one who threatens confirms his speech with an emphatic device, he has indicated that there is no leniency in his threat.

The origin of a'tadna is a'ddna, with two dals, meaning hayya'na (We made ready) for the disbelievers. It is said i'tadda just as it is said a'adda. God the Exalted said (﴿And she prepared for them a banquet﴾ [Yusuf: 31]).

The linguists (a'immat al-lughah) have hesitated over whether the root of the verb is with two dals or with a ta' and a dal, and they did not decide definitively which of the two is the origin, because the verb a'adda and the verb i'tadda occur very frequently in speech. The more apparent view is that they are two verbs that arose from two dialects, except that usage restricted the verb with the ta' to the "preparation for war" ('uddat al-harb), so they said 'ataad al-harb (the equipment of war) and did not say 'idad.

As for al-'uddah with a damma on the 'ayn, it applies to everything that is prepared and readied. It is said: a'adda li-kulli hal 'uddatan (he prepared a provision for every situation). The word al-'ataad is also applied to what is readied of matters.

Most often, when assimilation (idgham) is intended, the verb whose middle radical is a dal is used; and when there is a requirement for unassimilating (fakk al-idgham) due to a cause, such as the first-person pronoun, the verb whose middle radical is a ta' is used.

Al-salasil: the fetters made of rings of iron with which criminals and captives are bound.

Al-aghlal: the plural of ghull with a damma on the ghayn, which is a large ring of iron placed on the neck of the one who is bound, and to which the chain is attached. God the Exalted said (﴿When the shackles are on their necks and the chains﴾ [Ghafir: 71]). So the shackles and chains are placed on them when they are driven toward Hell.

Al-sa'ir: the kindled fire, i.e., that which the kindlers have set ablaze by adding more fuel so that its burning intensifies. It is, originally, a descriptive word in the sense of the passive participle, made a proper name for Hell. It has already been discussed at His saying (﴿Whenever it dies down, We increase them in blaze﴾ [al-Isra': 97]) in Surat al-Isra'.

The word (salasila) is written in the Imam Mushaf, in all the copies that were sent to the regions, with an alif after the second lam. However, the reciters differed in its recitation. Nafi', al-Kisa'i, Hisham from Ibn 'Amir, Abu Bakr from 'Asim, and Abu Ja'far recited (salasila) with tanwin when connected, and they stopped on it as one stops on a tanwin-ended accusative. Since its proper form is that it should be diptote (mamnu' min al-sarf), because it follows the pattern of the final plural forms, it becomes clear that its recitation with tanwin is for the sake of harmonizing (muzawajah) it with the two nouns that follow it, which are (﴿aghlalan﴾ [Ya-Sin: 8]) and (﴿sa'iran﴾ [al-Isra': 97]). Harmonization is a method in eloquent speech. Among its examples is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ to women: "Return with burdens (ma'zurat), not rewarded (ma'jurat)," where he made "ma'zurat" hamzated, whereas its proper form should be with a waw, but it was hamzated for the sake of harmonizing it with ma'jurat. Likewise his saying in the hadith of the two angels' questioning of the disbeliever: "It is said to him: You neither knew nor recited," whereas the original would be "wa la talawta." Among this is the verse of Ibn Muqbil or al-Qallah:

A destroyer of tents, an entrer of gates, mixing with him piety, its vigour and gentleness.

Here his saying "abwibah" is the plural of bab, and its proper form would be "abwab."

This recitation is sound, supported by the orthography of the Mushaf, and it proceeds in an eloquent Arabic manner. The rest read it without tanwin when connected.

They also differed in its recitation when pausing on it. Most of them recited it in pause without alif, saying (salasil) in pause. Abu 'Amr and Ruways from Ya'qub recited it with alif, treating it as tanwinated when connected.

al-Bazzi from Ibn Kathir, Ibn Dhakwan from Ibn 'Amir, and Hafs from 'Asim recited it in pause with both options permitted, with the alif and without it.

As for those who did not add tanwin to (salasila) when connected, and paused on it with an alif after its second lam, namely Abu 'Amr and Ruways from Ya'qub, the divergence of their transmission from the orthography of the Mushaf is explained by the fact that the orthography followed the state of pausing, and this is frequent. Writing the alif after the lam is intended to draw attention to lengthening the fatha at pause, for the harmonization of the closing rhyme (fawasil) at pause, since the fawasil are often given the rulings of qawafi and saj'.

Furthermore, the readings are transmitted narrations heard, and the orthography of the Mushaf is a specific tradition belonging to it. Al-Tibi mentioned that some scholars excused the difference of the reciters in His saying (salasila) by saying that it is from the difference in the manner of delivery, such as elongation (madd), inclination (imalah), and easing of the hamza, and that difference in these does not contradict mass transmission (tawatur).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 76, verses 5–6:

﴿Indeed, the righteous will drink from a cup whose mixture is camphor﴾ ﴿a spring from which the servants of Allah drink; they make it gush forth in abundance﴾. This is an explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani) arising from the preceding resumption, His saying (﴿Indeed, We have prepared for the disbelievers chains﴾ [al-Insan: 4]) etc. For whoever knows what has been prepared for the ungrateful of the recompense will long to know what has been prepared for the grateful of the reward.

The detailed account of it was delayed beyond the detailed account of the recompense of the ungrateful, although "grateful" (shakir) is mentioned before "ungrateful" (kafur), by way of the reversed method of laff wa nashr (wrapping and unfolding), so that there is room for an extended discourse on the attribute of the recompense of the grateful and what it contains of goodness and honour, bringing the described thing closer to direct sensory witnessing.

The emphasis of the report about the recompense of the grateful serves to repel the denial of the polytheists that the believers could be better than them in the world of eternity, and to convey concern with this glad tidings regarding the believers.

Al-abrar: they are the grateful. He expressed them as "the righteous" (al-abrar) to add praise for them.

Al-abrar is the plural of barr, with the fatha on the ba', and also the plural of barr (bar) like shahid and ashhad. Al-barr or al-bar is one who abounds in birr, with the kasra on the ba', and it is the doing of good. For this reason, al-barr is among the attributes of Allah the Exalted, as He said (﴿Indeed, We used to invoke Him before. Indeed, He is the Benefactor, the Merciful﴾ [al-Tur: 28]).

The description barr is stronger than barr (bar) in attributing righteousness, which is why one says "Allah is Barr," and one does not say "Allah is Bar."
Barr is pluralised as barara. It occurs in al-Raghib's Mufradat that barara is more eloquent than abrar.

The description of their bliss begins with the bliss of the pleasure of drinking from the wine of Paradise, because the pleasure of wine is well known among people, and they used to compete for obtaining it.

Al-ka's (cup), with the hamza, is the vessel prepared for wine; it is not called a cup unless wine is in it. Wine may also be called a cup by way of metonymy (majaz mursal) on this basis, as His saying the Exalted will soon come (﴿And they will be given to drink therein a cup whose mixture is ginger﴾ [al-Insan: 17]). So it is permissible that the vessels of wine be meant here, in which case min (from) is for the beginning of the source, and the singular "cup" is for the type; and it is permissible that wine be meant, in which case min is partitive.

On both interpretations, "cup" is meant as a genus, and its tanwin is for its magnification within its kind.

Al-mizaj, with the kasra on the mim, is what is mixed with something else, i.e., is blended. They used to mix wine with water when the wine was aged and strong, in order to lessen its sharpness. The mention of mixing wine occurs frequently in Arab poetry.

The pronoun in mizajuha refers back to ka's.

If the cup is meant as the vessel of wine, then the idafa is for the least connection, i.e., the mixture of what is in it; and if wine is meant, then the idafa is the idafa of the verbal noun to its object.

Al-kafur is an oil extracted from a tree resembling the oleander, which grows in the lands of China and Java; it forms in it when its duration is long, about two hundred years; its wood is boiled and an oil called kafur is extracted from it. It is thick and may harden so that it becomes like foam; and when the wood of the kafur tree falls into water, it becomes a nabidh that ferments and becomes intoxicating.

Kafur is white in colour, of pleasant fragrance, and refreshing.

It has been said that the mizaj here is meant as water, and that describing it as kafur is of the type of eloquent simile (tashbih baligh), i.e., in colour or the pleasantness of fragrance. Perhaps what led some exegetes to this is that

Page 381
the common practice among people regarding the fragrance of wine is to put musk on the rims of the bowl. Al-Nabigha said:

"It is poured when you wish, unmixed with bitterness, in a vessel whose rims hold musk, drinking."

Wine vessels are also sealed with a seal of musk, as in His saying concerning the people of Paradise (﴿They are given to drink of a sealed nectar, whose seal is musk﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 25]). They used to put pepper in wine for the pleasantness of its fragrance and the delightful burning sting of its heat on the tongue, as Imru' al-Qays said:

"They greeted us in the morning with pure wine, peppered."

It is possible that they mixed wine with water in which there was kafur, or with its oil, so that the mizaj in the verse is in its literal sense, that with which wine is mixed; and perhaps this was a custom of the people of luxury, because kafur is precious and is counted among perfumes.

Some exegetes said that kafur is the name of a spring in Paradise, because of His saying after it (﴿a spring from which the servants of Allah drink﴾). You will know the true meaning of it.

The insertion of the verb "kana" in the descriptive clause with His saying (﴿whose mixture was kafur﴾) is to convey that this is their mixture which never leaves it, since the common experience in this world is the rarity of that mixture because of its high price and scarcity of its availability.

"Eynan" (a spring) is in the accusative as a substitute (badal) for "kafuran", i.e., that kafur is what a spring in Paradise flows with, from water dissolved in it or from its oil, like His saying (﴿And rivers of milk whose taste does not change, and rivers of wine, delightful to drinkers, and rivers of purified honey﴾ [Muhammad: 15]). The verb "yashrabu" is transitive with the ba', which is the ba' of adhesion (ilsaq), because their drink is mixed with kafur. So the estimate is: a spring from which the servants of Allah drink their wine, i.e., accompanied by its water. Al-Asma'i went to the view that the ba' in His saying (﴿from which the servants of Allah drink﴾) has the meaning of partitive min, and al-Farisi, Ibn Qutayba and Ibn Malik agreed with him; Ibn Malik counted this among the meanings of ba' in his books, and it is attributed to the Kufans.

"Ibad Allah" (servants of Allah) is meant as: the righteous. It is an explicit noun in place of the pronoun, to honour them by attributing their servitude to Allah the Exalted, an attribution of honour.

Al-fajir: opening the earth for water, i.e., extracting abundant water; here it is applied to drawing from it without limit or depletion, so each one makes a spring gush forth for himself; and this is metaphor (isti'ara).

The verb in (﴿they make it gush forth in abundance﴾) is emphasised as a tarshih (nurturing) of the metaphor.

**Commentary of Ibn ʿAshur (al-Taḥrīr wa al-Tanwīr) on Surah 76, verse 7:**

﴿They fulfil the vow and fear a Day whose evil is widespread.﴾

This is an *iʿtirāḍ* (an interjected clause) placed between the clause ﴿they drink from a cup﴾ [al-Insān: 5] and the clause ﴿and vessels of silver will be passed around to them﴾ [al-Insān: 15]. This *iʿtirāḍ* is an *istiʾnāf bayānī* (an explanatory resumptive clause), that is, an answer to a question which the preceding discourse naturally raises in the mind of the listener who envies them, namely how he might attain the same bounty and honour in the Hereafter as they attained. So he is concerned to do what they did. Therefore God mentions some of their righteous deeds, which are among the fruits of faith, while alluding to the listener's need to increase in them in this world.

The statement is a report about them, issued at the time these verses were revealed. Part of it describes their state in the Hereafter, and part describes some of their state in this world, which is what made them deserving of what they attained in the Hereafter. Therefore there is no need for the view of al-Farrāʾ that the sentence contains an ellipsis, its supposed original form being: "they used to fulfil the vow."

The clause is not a *ḥāl* (circumstantial clause) relating to the righteous (al-abrār) or their pronoun, because a *ḥāl* is a qualifier of its governing verb. Had it been made a *ḥāl*, it would qualify ﴿yashrabūn﴾ (they drink). But their fulfilment of vows does not occur at the time they drink the wine of Paradise; rather it is by what they had sent ahead in the worldly life.

*Al-wafāʾ* (fulfilment) is the discharge of what is incumbent upon the one who discharges it, complete, without deficiency or negligence in it.

*Al-nadhr* (vow) is what a person resolves upon and fixes his intention on. ʿAntara said:

*"And the two vowers, if I do not meet them, my blood…"*

What is meant here is what they fixed their resolve upon of faith and obedience, which is what made them deserving of the description "the righteous" (al-abrār).

It is also possible that *al-nadhr* means what they vow of acts of goodness drawn near to God, that is, they initiate vows of these deeds in order to make them obligatory upon themselves.

The verb is in the present form (*yūfūna*) to indicate the renewal of their fulfilment of what their hearts have fixed upon of faith and righteous action. This implies that they frequently vow acts of obedience and perform acts of devotion. Had it not been so, fulfilment of the vow would not have been grounds for praise of them.

The definiteness in *al-nadhr* is the definiteness of genus (*taʿrīf al-jins*), so it encompasses every vow.

The clause ﴿and fear a Day whose evil is widespread﴾ is conjoined to ﴿they fulfil the vow﴾. Because they were described as acting upon what they vowed, God followed this with mention of the goodness of their intention and the sincerity of their deeds, since deeds are by intentions. Thus there were combined for them soundness of belief and goodness of deeds.

Their fear of "the Day" is a *majāz ʿaqlī* (rational metaphor), in that the attribution of the Day to the fear is figurative. They fear only what occurs on that Day of reckoning and of requital for evil deeds by punishment, so the act of fearing is linked to the time of the feared things.

*Yawman* (a Day) is in the accusative as the direct object of ﴿yakhāfūna﴾ (they fear). It cannot be in the accusative as an adverb of time (*ẓarf*), because what is meant by fear is their fear in this world of sins that lead them to punishment on that Day. It does not mean that they fear on that Day itself, since on that Day they are secure.

The Day is described as having an evil that is *mustaṭīr* (widespread), a description which indicates the cause of their fear of it. The meaning is: they fear the evil of that Day, so they avoid what leads them to its evil, namely the deeds for which punishment has been threatened.

*Al-sharr* (evil) is punishment and an evil recompense.

*Al-mustaṭīr* is an active participle of *istaṭāra*, which is intransitive. The *sīn* and *tāʾ* in *istaṭāra* are for intensification, and its root is *ṭāra*, like *istakbara*. Flying here is figurative, borrowed for the spreading and extension of a thing, likening it to the spreading of birds in the air. From this comes the expression "the widespread dawn" (*al-fajr al-mustaṭīr*), which is the true dawn whose light spreads across the horizon. It is also said: *istaṭāra al-ḥarīq* ("the fire spread") when it spread and followed one part after another.

The mention of the verb *kāna* (was) serves to indicate the firm establishment of the report concerning the one reported about. Otherwise, the evil of that Day is not an occurrence in the past; rather it will occur after a distant future. It is possible that this is an instance of expressing the future by a past form, to emphasise the certainty of its occurrence.

The form *yakhāfūna* (they fear) indicates the renewal of their fear of the evil of that Day, in the same manner as His saying ﴿they fulfil the vow﴾.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 76, verses 8–10:

﴿And they give food, in spite of their love for it, to the needy, the orphan, and the captive.﴾ ﴿We feed you only for the sake of Allah. We desire from you no reward nor thanks.﴾ ﴿Indeed, we fear from our Lord a Day austere and distressing.﴾

The giving of food is singled out for mention because in feeding the needy there is an element of preferring them over oneself, as His saying ﴿in spite of their love for it﴾ indicates. Stating the word "food" explicitly, although it is understood from the verb ﴿yut'imūn﴾ (Adh-Dhariyat: 57), serves as a preparation upon which the circumstantial phrase ﴿in spite of their love for it﴾ is built. For had it been said, "and they feed the needy, the orphan, and the captive," there would have been lost the meaning of preferring the destitute over oneself contained in His saying ﴿in spite of their love for it﴾. Moreover, mentioning "food" after ﴿yut'imūn﴾ gives emphasis while bringing to mind the state of feeding, so that it is as if the listener is witnessing the scene.

﴿In spite of their love for it﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl) from the pronoun in ﴿yut'imūn﴾.

ʿAlā (on/in spite of) here carries the meaning of maʿa (with), and the pronoun in ḥubbihi refers back to ṭaʿām (food), meaning: they feed food accompanied by their love for it, i.e., while being attached to their love for it. Love of food is the craving for it.

So the meaning is: they feed food that they themselves are in need of.

The use of ʿalā in the sense of maʿa arises from a kind of weakening of the sense of elevation (isti'lā'); its form is that the object of the particle ʿalā in such a construction is more excellent than the complement of its governed element, so it is treated as if it were something elevated upon.

The needy (miskīn) is the one in need. The orphan (yatīm) is one who has lost his father, and this is the usual cause of need, because the conditions of the Arabs were based on the father earning for the family through his toil; when the father is lost, the family is exposed to poverty.

As for the captive (asīr): since the whole surah is Meccan, before the might of the Muslims, the captive here means the Muslim slave, since the polytheists would starve their slaves who had embraced Islam, such as Bilal, ʿAmmar and his mother, and sometimes they would release some of them when their torture wearied them and leave them without provision.

Slavery arises from captivity, so the slave is a captive, and for this reason he is also called ʿānī. The Prophet ﷺ said, "Free the ʿānī," and he said concerning women, "Indeed they are ʿawān with you," in the manner of a comparison. Suḥaym, the slave of Banu al-Ḥisḥās, said:

She saw a worn saddle and a tattered turban, and a black, dusty one whom people deny to be a ʿānī (slave).

He means a slave. Al-Qurtubi cites from al-Tha'labi that Abu Sa'id al-Khudri said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited ﴿And they give food, in spite of their love for it, to the needy, the orphan, and the captive﴾ and said: "The miskīn is the poor person, the yatīm is the one who has no father, and the asīr is the enslaved and the imprisoned." I have not found the chain of this hadith.

From this you know that there is no evidence in this verse that the surah was revealed in Medina, or concerning the captives who were in the custody of the Muslims at the Battle of Badr.

The clause ﴿We feed you only for the sake of Allah﴾ through to its end is a quoted speech of an omitted saying, its implied form being: they say to them, i.e., to those whom they feed. It is thus in the position of a circumstantial phrase from the pronoun in ﴿yut'imūn﴾ (Adh-Dhariyat: 57). The clause ﴿We desire from you no reward nor thanks﴾ explains the content of the clause ﴿We feed you only for the sake of Allah﴾.

The clause ﴿Indeed, we fear from our Lord﴾ through to its end stands in the position of a reason for the content of the clause ﴿We desire from you no reward nor thanks﴾.

The meaning is: they say this to them to put them at ease and to remove the sense of humiliation that arises for the soul at the time of feeding, i.e., "We feed you only in compliance with what Allah has commanded, so it is Allah who is the true feeder of you."

So the saying is a saying with the tongue, and they say nothing except that it is concealed in their souls. From Mujahid: "They did not speak it, but Allah knew it, and so praised them for it."

The restriction derived from ʿinnamā is a restriction of correction (qaṣr qalb), based on treating the recipients as if they thought that the one who fed them would bestow favour upon them and desire from them recompense and thanks, according to what was customary among them in the Jahiliyyah. By recompense is meant what is a return for the gift, such as service or help; and by thanks is meant mentioning them with superiority.

Shukūr is a verbal noun on the pattern fuʿūl like quʿūd and julūs, and it is regarded as following the pattern fuʿūl which is the verbal noun of the intransitive faʿala, because the act of thanking does not usually take the one thanked as its direct object, but rather with the preposition lām; one says shakartu laka (I thanked you). Allah the Exalted says ﴿And be thankful to Me﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 152).

As for His saying ﴿Indeed, we fear from our Lord a Day austere and distressing﴾, it is a quoted speech of a saying that they say within their souls, or that some of them speak to others, and it is a circumstantial phrase from the pronoun in "yakhāfūn" (they fear), meaning: they fear that Day within their souls, saying ﴿Indeed, we fear from our Lord a Day austere and distressing﴾. Thus it is related, along with their saying ﴿We feed you only for the sake of Allah﴾ and their saying ﴿Indeed, we fear﴾ etc., in the manner of reversed "laff wa nashr" (wrapping and unfolding). The reason for reversing the order of unfolding is the aim of good arrangement of the composition, so that the transition is from mention of feeding to what they say to those fed, and the transition is from mention of fear of the Day of Reckoning to the good news of Allah's protection of them from the evil of that Day and what they will meet in it of radiance, joy and bliss.

So it is permissible that ﴿from our Lord﴾ be a settled adverbial phrase, with min being initial (ibtidā'iyyah), and it is a circumstantial phrase from "yawman" which is placed before it, meaning: we fear a Day austere and distressing, being of the days of our Lord, i.e., of His dispositions.

It is also permissible that min be partitive/abstractive (tajrīdiyyah), as in your saying: "From so-and-so I have a close friend." Then "yawman" is accusative as an adverb of time, and its tanwīn is for magnification, meaning: we fear it on a severe day.

"ʿAbūsan" is accusative as an object of the verb "nakhāf," meaning: we fear a wrathful one, very fierce in wrath, who is our Lord; so in the abstraction there is a strengthening of fear, since it is like fear of two things, and this is the point of the abstraction. Or "ʿabūsan" is a circumstantial phrase from "min rabbinā."

It is also permissible to make min serve to transitivise the verb "nakhāf," as it is transitivised in His saying ﴿Then whoever fears from a testator injustice﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 182). "Yawman" is then accusative as the direct object of the verb "nakhāf," so that the verb "nakhāf" has two objects. And "ʿabūsan" is an adjective of "yawman," and the meaning is: we fear the punishment of a Day having this description, so in it there is an emphasis on fear by repeating its object, and the repetition returns to it being the fear of Allah, because the Day is the Day of Allah's justice and judgment.

ʿAbūs is an adjective of the pattern of the stable attribute for one who is intensely stern-faced, i.e., a contraction of the face and its not relaxing. The description of the Day as ʿabūs is by way of metaphor: the Day in which events occur that displease them is likened to a man who associates with them and is harsh of character, stern in his dealings.

Qamṭarīr: the very severe and difficult of everything. From Ibn ʿAbbas: qamṭarīr is the one whose brow is contracted [between his eyes], derived from qamṭara (intransitive) when it gathers together, or qamṭara (transitive) when he tied the waterskin with a string or the like; from it the case in which books are placed is called qimṭar, and it is like a satchel. The mīm of qamṭarīr is original, so its pattern is fa'lalīl like khandarīs and zanjabīl; it is said: qimṭar for evil, when one prepares for it and gathers oneself.

The majority have made "qamṭarīran" a description of "yawman," and some have made it a description of "ʿabūsan," meaning very stern.

This verse encompasses all the righteous (abrār), and upon this its fabric is woven. The storytellers and preachers have seized upon it, fabricating various tales for it and bringing fabricated reports and invented verses. Among them is one who claimed that this verse was revealed concerning ʿAli ibn Abi Talib and Fatimah, may Allah be pleased with them both, in a lengthy story which al-Tha'labi and al-Naqqash related, and which al-Qurtubi cited in full and then refuted. It is reported from al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi that he said in Nawadir al-Usul: this is a fabricated and falsified narration, and it resembles being one of the narrations of the people of prisons.

It was also said that it was revealed concerning Mut'im ibn Waraqa al-Ansari, and it was said concerning another man from the Ansar. Al-Qurtubi has fully covered all of that in his tafsir, so there is no benefit in bringing it up. The Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and his family are worthy that the Qur'an should be revealed concerning them, but these reports are weak or fabricated.

Moreover, mentioning "food" after ﴿yut'imūn﴾ gives emphasis while bringing to mind the state of feeding, so that it is as if the listener is witnessing the scene.

﴿In spite of their love for it﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl) from the pronoun in ﴿yut'imūn﴾.

The needy (miskīn) is the one in need. The orphan (yatīm) is one who has lost his father, and this is the usual cause of need, because the conditions of the Arabs were based on the father earning for the family through his toil; when the father is lost, the family is exposed to poverty.

He means a slave. I have not found the chain of this hadith.

From this you know that there is no evidence in this verse that the surah was revealed in Medina, or concerning the captives who were in the custody of the Muslims at the Battle of Badr.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 76, verses 11–14:

﴿So Allah protected them from the evil of that Day and gave them radiance and joy.﴾ ﴿And He rewarded them, for what they endured, with a Garden and silk.﴾ ﴿Reclining therein upon couches, they will see therein neither sun nor bitter cold.﴾ ﴿And near them will be its shade, and its clusters will be lowered in readiness.﴾

This is a continuation of His saying (﴿They fulfil their vows﴾ [al-Insan: 7]) up to (﴿a hard, distressing day﴾ [al-Insan: 10]).

In this continuation there is a shift in the discourse about the reward of the righteous and the people of gratitude. This is a barzakh (bridge, transitional passage) leading to a return to the speech on the excellence of their reward: that Allah protected them from the evil of that Day, which is the far-spreading evil mentioned just before. He protected them from it as a reward for their fear of it, and that He gave them radiance and joy as a reward for the good they did.

Included within this is His saying (﴿for what they endured﴾), which encompasses all the states of piety and righteous deeds, because all of them involve the self bearing up to abandon what is loved or to perform something burdensome, and among that is feeding food despite love for it.

Laqqahum means: He made them encounter radiance and joy, i.e., He made for them radiance, which is beauty of complexion, and this comes from the soul's joy and the ease of living. Allah the Exalted said (﴿Faces that Day will be radiant﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 22]). Thus the casting of radiance upon their faces is depicted as one person being thrust toward meeting another, in the manner of metaphorical depiction (tamthil).

The feminine pronoun and (radiance) are the two objects of laqqa, which follows the pattern of kasa (to clothe, taking two objects).

Between waqahum and laqqahum there is a paronomasia of the imperfect type (al-jinas al-muharraf).

The clause (﴿and He rewarded them, for what they endured, with a Garden and silk﴾) is coordinated with the clause "fawaqahum" and the clause "wa laqqahum," because the three clauses are alike in being verbal and in the past tense; these two are among the embellishments of connection (muhassinat al-wasl).

Al-harir (silk): a name for threads from the secretions of a particular worm; its discussion was preceded in Surat Fatir.

The reward was in ease of living, since He placed them in the finest dwellings, which is the Garden, and clothed them in the finest garments, which is silk, which only people of great wealth wear. Thus there was gathered for them the beauty of the external container and the beauty of the immediate container, which is clothing.

What is meant by harir here is that which is woven from it.

Muttaki'in (reclining) is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the plural pronoun in jazahum, i.e., they are in the Garden reclining upon couches.

Al-ittika' (reclining): a posture between sitting and lying down, in which the one seated leans on his elbow and side and stretches out his legs, and it is a posture of ease. It was a mark of kings and people of luxury. For this reason the Prophet ﷺ said: "As for me, I do not eat reclining." This was discussed previously in Surat Yusuf at His saying (﴿and she prepared for them a couch﴾ [Yusuf: 31]).

Al-araik is the plural of arika, on the pattern of safina. The arika is a bed with a cushion and a curtain with it, which is its canopy (hajalah). The hajalah, with two fathas and with the unpointed ha' preceding the jim: a light curtain hung above the bed to protect from heat and sun. A bed is not called arika unless it has a canopy with it.

It has been said: everything used as a pillow or spread out which has stuffing is called arika, even if it has no canopy. In al-Itqan, from Ibn al-Jawzi: that the arika is the bed in Abyssinian (Habashi). Al-Suyuti added this to the verses of Ibn al-Subki and Ibn Hajar in the collection of Arabic loanwords in the Qur'an.

The clause (﴿they will see therein neither sun nor bitter cold﴾) is a second circumstantial clause from the pronoun of absence in (jazahum), or an adjective of (jannah).

By the sun is meant the heat of its rays. He negated seeing the sun in His saying (﴿they will see therein no sun﴾), so the negation of seeing the sun is a kinaya (metonymy) for negating the existence of the sun, which entails the absence of the heat of its rays. It is thus of the allusive metonymy (al-kinaya al-talwihiyya), like his saying:

"And you do not see the lizard therein retreating into its burrow."
That is: there is no lizard there that you would see, and there is no retreating into burrows.

Al-zamharir: a name for strong cold in the dialect of the Hijaz. Al-zamharir is also a name for cold.

The meaning: the air of the Garden is moderate, with no pain in it in any way. And in the speech of the fourth of the women in the hadith of Umm Zar': "My husband is like the night of Tihama: neither hot nor cold, neither fearful nor weary."

Tha'lab said: al-zamharir is the name of the moon in the dialect of Tayy, and he recited:

"And a night whose darkness has grown dense, I crossed it while the zamharir had not shone."

The meaning according to this: that they will not see in the Garden the light of the sun nor the light of the moon, i.e., the light of day and the light of night, because the radiance of the Garden is from one singular light specific to it. This is a meaning other than the negation of heat and cold.

Among the people is one who says: what is meant by the sun is its actual essence, and by zamharir is cold, and that in the speech there is ihtibak (interlocking ellipsis), the estimate being: they will not see therein a sun, nor a moon, nor heat, nor bitter cold. They made this an example of ihtibak among the badi' embellishments. Perhaps his intention is that the meaning is that its light is moderate and its air is moderate.

(﴿And near them will be its shade﴾) "Daniyatan" is in the accusative, coordinated with "muttaki'in," because this is a causal circumstance of the reclining ones, i.e., the shades of the trees of the Garden are near them. "Zilaluha" is the subject of daniyah, and the pronoun in zilaluha refers to jannah.

The nearness of the shades: their closeness to them. Since the description of shade with nearness is not customary, this shows that the nearness of the shades is a metonymy for the drooping of the branches which in the customary world of this life would shade the gardens; but since the Garden has no sun from whose heat one shelters, it is determined that the construction (﴿near them its shades﴾) is an idiom applied to the drooping of the branches of the Garden, because the shade cast on a person does not vary by nearness or distance. It may also be that "zilaluha" is a metonymy (majaz mursal) for the branches by the relation of necessity.

The meaning: the boughs of the Garden are close to their sitting places, and this increases its splendor and beauty, and it is in the sense of His saying (﴿its fruit-clusters are near﴾ [al-Haqqah: 23]).

For this reason He coordinated with it the clause (﴿and its clusters will be lowered in readiness﴾), i.e., the clusters of those boughs were made subservient to them and made easy for them, such that there is no bending in them nor hardness that would tire the one who picks them, and they do not stretch toward them, but gather them with the easiest reach.

Thus "tadhlil" is borrowed for facilitation, as one says: a horse that is dhalul, i.e., obedient to its rider; and a cow that is dhalul, i.e., trained to work. This was discussed in Surat al-Baqarah.

Al-qutuf: plural of qitf, with a kasra on the qaf and a sukun on the ta', which is a cluster of dates or grapes. It was called qitf in a form of the passive participle, like dhibh, because one intends to pick it; so applying "qitf" to it is a metaphor based on what it becomes, which has become common in speech. The pronoun in "qutufuha" refers to jannah, or to its shades, considering the shades as a metonymy for the trees.

"Tadhlilan" is a verbal noun emphasizing that, i.e., intense, complete subjection.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 76, verse 15–16:

[391]
﴿And there will be circulated among them vessels of silver and cups that were [made of] glass.﴾ ﴿Glass of silver, which they have determined in [precise] measure.﴾

This is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon the clause (﴿They will drink from a cup﴾ [al-Insan: 5]) and so forth, as the parallelism required between the clause "yashrabun" (they drink) and the clause (﴿They will be circulated among them﴾ [al-Saffat: 45]) in being a verbal sentence (fiʿliyyah) and in its present-tense form (mudariʿiyyah). This is among the best forms of connection (wasl). The discourse returns to describing the settings of their drinking.

This clause is an explanation (bayan) of what was stated in summary in the clause (﴿Indeed, the righteous will drink from a cup﴾ [al-Insan: 5]). It is conjoined to what precedes it because of the difference it contains from the conjoined clause, which concerns the description of the vessels of drink. For this reason, after mentioning the gatherings and reclining couches of the people of Paradise, it follows with a mention of what naturally accompanies these, namely what the people of this world know of the states of the people of luxury, opulence and pleasures, through drinking wine, when attendants circulate the vessels of wine among them. Since this was well known, there was no need to mention the agent of the circulating, so it was made passive (bunya lil-naʾib).

This is a promise to them of the granting of what they desired in this world, together with an increase upon it of the bliss of Paradise, "which no eye has seen, nor has it occurred to the heart of any human."

Al-tawaf (circulation) is repeated walking around something or between things. Since the people reclining were a group, the attendant's going around among them is called tawaf. They have named the serving of wine "circulating the wine" or "circulating the cup." The one who serves (al-saqi) is the one who circulates the cup, or the one who circulates the goblet, or the like.

Al-aniyah (vessels) is the plural of inaʾ, a lengthened form on the pattern af ʿila, like kisaʾ and akhsiyah, wiʿaʾ and awʿiyah; two hamzas came together at the beginning of the plural, one added and one original, so the second was softened into an alif.

Al-inaʾ is the name for every container used for practical purposes. Al-Raghib said: "That in which a thing is placed." It appears that it applies to every container intended for use and handling for foods, drinks and the like, whether it is of wood, metal, earthenware, leather or glass, in which what is drunk or eaten is placed, or in which it is cooked. Apparently it is not applied to what is made for storage; a waterskin is not an inaʾ, nor is a large jar (al-batiyah) an inaʾ. The cup (kaʾs) is an inaʾ, the mug (kuz) is an inaʾ, the ewer (ibriq) is an inaʾ, and the dish (sahfah) is an inaʾ.

What is meant here is the vessels of their drinking gatherings, as the mention of the cups indicates, and this is within the general sense of vessels and what is placed with them of platters, roasted meat or the like, as God said in the verse of al-Zukhruf: (﴿They will be circulated among them with dishes of gold and cups﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 71]).

[392]
The vessels include the goblets. The mention of "vessels" after "cup" in His saying (﴿Indeed, the righteous will drink from a cup﴾ [al-Insan: 5]) is mention of the general after the specific, unless by "cup" is meant the wine itself.

Al-akwab is the plural of kub, with a damma on the kaf followed by a silent waw. Al-kub is a mug without a handle and without a spout, and this was discussed in surah al-Zukhruf.

The conjunction of "akwab" upon "aniyah" is the conjunction of the specific upon the general, because the cups are the vessels in which wine is carried to refill the goblets. It is described here as being of silver, meaning their vessels come to them of silver at some times and of gold at other times, as indicated by His saying in surah al-Zukhruf (﴿with dishes of gold and cups﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 71]), since gold has its beauty and silver has its beauty; so their vessels are made of the two precious metals so that they do not miss the beauty and loveliness of each. Or it means they are circulated among them with vessels of silver and vessels of gold, varied and matched, since that is more radiant in appearance, just as He said once (﴿And they will be adorned with bracelets of silver﴾ [al-Insan: 21]) and once (﴿They will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold﴾ [al-Kahf: 31]). This brings delight to their souls through the beauty of the sights, for they used to wish for these in this world because of their rarity or the abundance of them. The mention of silver vessels is emphasized here because of the comparison of them to glass in whiteness.

Al-qawarir is the plural of qarurah. The original meaning of qarurah is a vessel resembling a mug. It has been said that it is not called qarurah unless it is of glass; and it has been said that it is used without restriction, and this is what the author of al-Qamus began with.

It is named qarurah derived from qarar, which is staying in a place; and this is a rare morphological pattern.

The usual sense of the name qarurah is a vessel of glass, though it may be applied to what is of glass even if it is not a vessel, as in His saying (﴿He said, "It is a palace paved with glass"﴾ [al-Naml: 44]). And the phrase "qawarira" in this verse has been explained as meaning that they are like glass in clarity of color and thinness, so that they almost show through what is in them.

The competition over the thinness of wine vessels is well known among its drinkers. Al-Aʿsha said:

It shows you the dregs beyond it, while it is beneath them; when one who tastes it tastes it, he smacks his lips.

The verb "kanat" here is an eloquent simile (tashbih baligh). The meaning is: they are like glass in their transparency. The indication of this is His saying "of silver" (﴿of silver﴾), meaning they are of the substance of silver in the color of glass, because His saying "of silver" is literal, since He said before it "with vessels of silver."

The second word "qawarira" may be a verbal emphasis (taʾkid lafdhi) of its counterpart, to increase the confirmation that it has the thinness of glass; in that case the pause is on the first "qawarira."

It may also be a repetition to indicate arrangement, since good ordering of the vessels of drink is among the things that complete the splendor of the gathering; in that case the repetition is like His saying (﴿And the angel in rows, row upon row﴾ [al-Fajr: 22]) and the people's saying, "I read the book chapter by chapter." In that case the pause is on the second "qawarira."

In the Mushaf it is written "qawarira qawarira" with an alif at the end of both words, which is the sign of tanwin.

Nafiʿ, al-Kisa'i, Abu Bakr from ʿAsim and Abu Jaʿfar read both the first and second "qawarira" with tanwin. The tanwin of the first is to match the words at the endings of the preceding and following verses, from His saying "kafuran" to "taqdiran"; the tanwin of the second is for matching with its counterpart. These readers also paused on both with the alif, like their counterparts, and a similar case has been mentioned in His saying (﴿chains and shackles﴾ [al-Insan: 4]).

Ibn Kathir, Khalaf and Ruways from Yaʿqub read the first "qawarira" with tanwin and paused on it with the alif, and this is consistent with the line of justification by which we justified the reading of Nafiʿ and al-Kisa'i. They read the second "qawarira" without tanwin, according to the original form, not observing the matching, and they paused on it with a sukun.

Ibn ʿAmir, Abu ʿAmr, Hamzah and Hafs from ʿAsim read both without tanwin, because of the prohibition of diptote inflection (mana' al-sarf), and without observing the verse endings or the matching.

The readings are mutawatir narrations, and the script of the Mushaf does not contradict them; perhaps those who wrote the codices had only received the reading of the people of Madinah.

Khalaf narrated from Yahya ibn Adam from Ibn Idris, who said: "In the early codices, the first 'qawarira' was established with an alif and the second without an alif," meaning the codices that were in Kufa, for ʿAbd Allah ibn Idris was Kufan. Abu ʿUbayd said: "I saw in the Mushaf of ʿUthman 'qawarira' the first with an alif, and the second was written with an alif, but it was scraped out, and I saw its trace there clearly." This statement is not useful; for even if it were sound, it would not be known who wrote it with an alif, nor who erased the alif, nor when that happened between the time the codices were written and the time of Abu ʿUbayd, nor is it known what is meant by "the Mushaf of ʿUthman": is it his personal codex that he was specially associated with, or is it one of the codices that were copied in his caliphate and which he distributed to the regions?

Yaʿqub read both without tanwin in pausal and continuous recitation alike in connected speech. In pausal recitation, Hamzah paused on both without an alif. Hisham from Ibn ʿAmir paused on both with an alif, considering it a extension (silah) of the fatha, that is, a lengthening of the fatha. Abu ʿAmr, Hafs and Ibn Dhakwan from Ibn ʿAmir, and Ruways from Yaʿqub paused on the first with an alif and on the second without an alif; its justification is that by which we justified the reading of Ibn Kathir and Khalaf.

His saying (﴿They have determined it in [precise] measure﴾) may mean that the plural pronoun refers to the righteous, or to (﴿the servants of God﴾ [al-Insan: 6]), to whom the preceding pronouns in His saying "yufajjiruna-ha" and "yufuna" and onward refer; the meaning of "determined" is then their desire that it come in accordance with what they wish.

It may also mean the pronoun refers to the implied deputy-subject of the passive "yutaf," that is, those who circulate among them with them determined the vessels and the cups, meaning they determined what is in them of drink according to what each drinker among them requests; and this returns in meaning to the first possibility. It was customary, among what is considered in ordinary practice a mark of the skill of the server, to give each person of the drink what suits his desire.

"Taqdiran" is an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) emphasizing its verb, to indicate the fulfillment of the measure, neither exceeding what is requested nor falling short of it.

What is meant here is the vessels of their drinking gatherings, as the mention of the cups indicates, and this is within the general sense of vessels and what is placed with them of platters, roasted meat or the like, as God said in the verse of al-Zukhruf: (﴿They will be circulated among them with dishes of gold and cups﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 71]).

[392]
The vessels include the goblets. The mention of "vessels" after "cup" in His saying (﴿Indeed, the righteous will drink from a cup﴾ [al-Insan: 5]) is mention of the general after the specific, unless by "cup" is meant the wine itself.

Al-akwab is the plural of kub, with a damma on the kaf followed by a silent waw. Al-kub is a mug without a handle and without a spout, and this was discussed in surah al-Zukhruf.

The conjunction of "akwab" upon "aniyah" is the conjunction of the specific upon the general, because the cups are the vessels in which wine is carried to refill the goblets. It is described here as being of silver, meaning their vessels come to them of silver at some times and of gold at other times, as indicated by His saying in surah al-Zukhruf (﴿with dishes of gold and cups﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 71]), since gold has its beauty and silver has its beauty; so their vessels are made of the two precious metals so that they do not miss the beauty and loveliness of each. Or it means they are circulated among them with vessels of silver and vessels of gold, varied and matched, since that is more radiant in appearance, just as He said once (﴿And they will be adorned with bracelets of silver﴾ [al-Insan: 21]) and once (﴿They will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold﴾ [al-Kahf: 31]). This brings delight to their souls through the beauty of the sights, for they used to wish for these in this world because of their rarity or the abundance of them. The mention of silver vessels is emphasized here because of the comparison of them to glass in whiteness.

Al-qawarir is the plural of qarurah. The original meaning of qarurah is a vessel resembling a mug. It has been said that it is not called qarurah unless it is of glass; and it has been said that it is used without restriction, and this is what the author of al-Qamus began with.

It is named qarurah derived from qarar, which is staying in a place; and this is a rare morphological pattern.

The usual sense of the name qarurah is a vessel of glass, though it may be applied to what is of glass even if it is not a vessel, as in His saying (﴿He said, "It is a palace paved with glass"﴾ [al-Naml: 44]). And the phrase "qawarira" in this verse has been explained as meaning that they are like glass in clarity of color and thinness, so that they almost show through what is in them.

The competition over the thinness of wine vessels is well known among its drinkers. Al-Aʿsha said:

It shows you the dregs beyond it, while it is beneath them; when one who tastes it tastes it, he smacks his lips.

The verb "kanat" here is an eloquent simile (tashbih baligh). The meaning is: they are like glass in their transparency. The indication of this is His saying "of silver" (﴿of silver﴾), meaning they are of the substance of silver in the color of glass, because His saying "of silver" is literal, since He said before it "with vessels of silver."

The second word "qawarira" may be a verbal emphasis (taʾkid lafdhi) of its counterpart, to increase the confirmation that it has the thinness of glass; in that case the pause is on the first "qawarira."

It may also be a repetition to indicate arrangement, since good ordering of the vessels of drink is among the things that complete the splendor of the gathering; in that case the repetition is like His saying (﴿And the angel in rows, row upon row﴾ [al-Fajr: 22]) and the people's saying, "I read the book chapter by chapter." In that case the pause is on the second "qawarira."

In the Mushaf it is written "qawarira qawarira" with an alif at the end of both words, which is the sign of tanwin.

Nafiʿ, al-Kisa'i, Abu Bakr from ʿAsim and Abu Jaʿfar read both the first and second "qawarira" with tanwin. The tanwin of the first is to match the words at the endings of the preceding and following verses, from His saying "kafuran" to "taqdiran"; the tanwin of the second is for matching with its counterpart. These readers also paused on both with the alif, like their counterparts, and a similar case has been mentioned in His saying (﴿chains and shackles﴾ [al-Insan: 4]).

Ibn Kathir, Khalaf and Ruways from Yaʿqub read the first "qawarira" with tanwin and paused on it with the alif, and this is consistent with the line of justification by which we justified the reading of Nafiʿ and al-Kisa'i. They read the second "qawarira" without tanwin, according to the original form, not observing the matching, and they paused on it with a sukun.

Ibn ʿAmir, Abu ʿAmr, Hamzah and Hafs from ʿAsim read both without tanwin, because of the prohibition of diptote inflection (mana' al-sarf), and without observing the verse endings or the matching.

The readings are mutawatir narrations, and the script of the Mushaf does not contradict them; perhaps those who wrote the codices had only received the reading of the people of Madinah.

Khalaf narrated from Yahya ibn Adam from Ibn Idris, who said: "In the early codices, the first 'qawarira' was established with an alif and the second without an alif," meaning the codices that were in Kufa, for ʿAbd Allah ibn Idris was Kufan. Abu ʿUbayd said: "I saw in the Mushaf of ʿUthman 'qawarira' the first with an alif, and the second was written with an alif, but it was scraped out, and I saw its trace there clearly." This statement is not useful; for even if it were sound, it would not be known who wrote it with an alif, nor who erased the alif, nor when that happened between the time the codices were written and the time of Abu ʿUbayd, nor is it known what is meant by "the Mushaf of ʿUthman": is it his personal codex that he was specially associated with, or is it one of the codices that were copied in his caliphate and which he distributed to the regions?

Yaʿqub read both without tanwin in pausal and continuous recitation alike in connected speech. In pausal recitation, Hamzah paused on both without an alif. Hisham from Ibn ʿAmir paused on both with an alif, considering it a extension (silah) of the fatha, that is, a lengthening of the fatha. Abu ʿAmr, Hafs and Ibn Dhakwan from Ibn ʿAmir, and Ruways from Yaʿqub paused on the first with an alif and on the second without an alif; its justification is that by which we justified the reading of Ibn Kathir and Khalaf.

His saying (﴿They have determined it in [precise] measure﴾) may mean that the plural pronoun refers to the righteous, or to (﴿the servants of God﴾ [al-Insan: 6]), to whom the preceding pronouns in His saying "yufajjiruna-ha" and "yufuna" and onward refer; the meaning of "determined" is then their desire that it come in accordance with what they wish.

It may also mean the pronoun refers to the implied deputy-subject of the passive "yutaf," that is, those who circulate among them with them determined the vessels and the cups, meaning they determined what is in them of drink according to what each drinker among them requests; and this returns in meaning to the first possibility. It was customary, among what is considered in ordinary practice a mark of the skill of the server, to give each person of the drink what suits his desire.

"Taqdiran" is an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) emphasizing its verb, to indicate the fulfillment of the measure, neither exceeding what is requested nor falling short of it.

**[Page 395]**

He follows the description of the vessels and their excellence with a description of the drink they contain and its fragrance. The *ka’s* (cup) here is a cup of wine, and it belongs to the general category of the vessels mentioned earlier, though it is not called a vessel of wine. It is only called a *ka’s* if wine is in it. The presence of wine in it is what makes it correct to call it a *ka’s*. For this reason it is fitting that the verb of giving drink is connected directly to the *ka’s*, because the concept of the *ka’s* is established by the wine in the vessel. Similar to this is the verse of al-A‘sha:

*And a cup I drank with delight, and another by which I treated myself.*

He means: and wine I drank.

The discussion of applying the term *ka’s* to the vessel, or to what is in it, is the same as the discussion of its counterpart mentioned earlier in His saying (﴿Indeed, the righteous will drink from a cup whose mixture is camphor﴾ [al-Insan: 5]).

The meaning of the verse is that this is another kind of drink. That is, at one time they drink from a cup whose mixture is camphor, and at another time they are given a cup whose mixture is ginger.

The pronoun in (*fīhā*, "in it") refers to the Garden mentioned in His saying (﴿a Garden and silk﴾ [al-Insan: 12]).

*Zanjabīl* (ginger) is an arabicized word, and its original form had the non-Arabic *kāf* in place of the *jīm*. Al-Jawaliqi and al-Tha‘alibi said: it is Persian, and it is the name of roots like the roots of *su‘d* (cyperus), with a *ḍamma* on the *sīn* and a sukun on the *‘ayn*, found in the earth like fine carrot and fine turnip. Its color tends toward white. It has a plant with a flower. It has a pleasant, fragrant smell, and its taste resembles pepper. It grows in the lands of China, Sind, Oman, and al-Shihr. It has varieties, the best of which grows in the lands of China. It enters medicines and cooking as a spice. Its aroma is like that of spices, and its taste is pungent. It is stimulating, and it is used steeped in water and preserved with sugar.

The Arabs knew it, and the poets of the Arabs mentioned it in connection with fragrant scent.

That is, they mix the wine with water in which ginger has been steeped, for the goodness of its scent and the pleasantness of its taste.

*‘Aynan* (a spring) is in the accusative as a substitute (*badal*) for *zanjabīlan*, as was mentioned earlier in His saying (﴿whose mixture was camphor﴾ [al-Insan: 5]) (﴿a spring from which the servants of God drink﴾ [al-Insan: 6]).

The meaning of ginger being a *‘ayn* (spring) is that its steeped liquid, or the drink extracted from it, is abundant, like a spring, in the manner of His saying (﴿and rivers of milk whose taste never changes﴾ [Muhammad: 15]). That is, it is very plentiful, and it was known in the world for its prestige.

**[Page 396]**

*Salsabīl*: it is a descriptive term, said to be derived from *salāsa*, which means ease and softness. One says: *māʼ salsal*, meaning sweet and cold water. It is said that the *bāʼ* and the *yāʼ* were added to it, that is, they were added to the original form without analogy.

Al-Tabrizi said in his commentary on the *Hamasa*, regarding the verse of al-Ba‘ith ibn Hurayth:

*A phantom for the mother of Salsabil, and between them a journey of a month for the wandering courier.*

Abu al-‘Ala’ said: *al-salsabīl* is water that is easy to swallow. In my view, this descriptive term is composed of the two roots *salāsa* and *sabāla*. One says: *sabalat al-samāʼ* when it rains. So *sabīl* is *faʻīl* in the sense of *mafʻūl*, composed of the two words *salāsa* and *sabīl*, to indicate the ease of drinking it and the abundance of its flow. This is from *al-ishtiqāq al-akbar* (the greater derivation), and it is not a derivation by morphological change (*ishtiqāq taṣrīfī*).

This is therefore a descriptive term from the language of the Arabs according to the verifying scholars of the people of language. Ibn al-A‘rabi said: I have not heard this word except in the Qur’an. So in his view it is one of the original coinages of the Qur’an that proceed according to the patterns of Arabic speech. In the margin of al-Hamadhani’s commentary on the *Kashshaf*, the verse of al-Ba‘ith mentioned above, together with two verses after it, is attributed to Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt. This is a strange attribution, and no one else has said it.

The meaning of *tusammā* (is named) on this view is that it is described by this description, until it became like a proper name for it, as He, the Exalted, said (﴿they name the angels with the name of females﴾ [al-Najm: 27]), that is, they describe them as females. From this is His saying, the Exalted (﴿Do you know of anyone with His name?﴾ [Maryam: 65]), that is, no one equal to Him. So the intended meaning is not that it is a proper name.

Some of the exegetes took the naming in its apparent sense, and made *Salsabīl* a proper name for this spring. This is more fitting with His saying, the Exalted, *tusammā*. According to the view of Ibn al-A‘rabi and the majority, there is no difficulty regarding the *tanwīn* (nunation) of *Salsabīl*. As for al-Jawaliqi, he said it is non-Arabic and was named by it, and its *tanwīn* is for the sake of harmonizing with the rhyme, like the *tanwīn* of *salāsila*.

This description resolves in hearing into two words: *sal* and *sabīlan*, that is, ask for a way. Some exegetes explained it this way, and it was mentioned that it was made a proper name for this spring as a kind of proper name transferred from a phrase, such as *Ta’abbaṭa sharran* and *Dharrā ḥabban*. In the *Kashshaf* it is said that this is far-fetched and an innovation.
