Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 76, verse 19:

Page 397
﴿And there will circulate among them young boys made eternal, who, when you see them, you would think them scattered pearls.﴾

This is another circulating (ṭawāf) different from the circulating of the cupbearers mentioned just before, by His saying: ﴿And there will be circulated among them vessels of silver﴾ [al-Insan: 15], etc. This is a circulating for the performance of service, so it includes the circulating of the cupbearers and others.

And "wildān" (young boys) is the plural of "walīd." The original form of walīd is faʿīl in the sense of mafʿūl, and "al-walīd" is used for a young child by a well-known metaphor (majāz), with the relation of "what was" (ʿalāqat mā kāna), intended to bring near the time of his birth. The best of those who are taken for service are the wildān, because they are the lightest in movement and the swiftest in walking, and because the one served feels no awkwardness in commanding them or forbidding them.

They are described as "mukhalladūn" (made eternal) as a safeguard against what the derivation of "wildān" might suggest, namely that they grow up and become middle-aged. That is, their attributes do not change; they are young boys perpetually. Otherwise, the eternity of the beings in Paradise is already known, so their mention was only for the sake of a specific kind of eternity.

Abu 'Ubayda said: "mukhalladūn" means "adorned with the khilda," on the pattern of qirada. Its singular is khuld, like qufl, and it is the name for an earring in the dialect of Himyar.

They were compared to scattered pearls in a restricted simile (tashbīh muqayyad), in which the compared is restricted to a particular state, because they were compared to them in beauty of appearance together with being spread out.

The construction "idhā ra'aytahum ḥasibtahum" ("when you see them, you would think them") conveys the intended simile, the intended sense being resemblance. The address in "ra'ayta" is addressed to an unspecified person, meaning: when anyone who sees them looks.

The discussion of the meaning of circulating has already been given at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And there will be circulated among them vessels of silver﴾ [al-Insan: 15], and so on.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 76, verse 20:

﴿And when you look there, you will see bliss and a great dominion.﴾

The address is to an unspecified person. "Tham" (there) is a demonstrative of place and is used only as an adverb of place. What is pointed to here is what has already been mentioned, namely the Garden mentioned in His saying: ﴿And He will reward them for what they endured with a garden and silk﴾ [al-Insan: 12].

Page 398

The first verb "ra'ayta" (you see) is treated as intransitive (munazzal manzilat al-lazim), indicating only the occurrence of sight, not its connection to a seen object; that is, when you direct your gaze. The second "ra'ayta" is the response (jawab) of "idha" (when), meaning: when you open your eyes, you will see bliss.

The restriction by "idha" conveys the sense of a condition, which indicates that the seeing of bliss does not fail to reach the eye of the one who sees there. Thus it conveys the meaning: you will see nothing but bliss, in contrast to what is seen in the regions of this world.

In His saying ﴿and a great dominion﴾ there is an eloquent simile (tashbih baligh), meaning: like the conditions of a great dominion enjoyed in comfort.

The benefit of this simile is to bring the thing compared closer to the faculties of the intellects.

"Kabir" (great) is used metaphorically for magnification, and it exceeds "bliss" by what it contains of elevation and the subduing of difficulties.

﴿Upon them will be garments of green silk and brocade, and they will be adorned with bracelets of silver﴾ (Al-Insan: 21). These are among the garments of kings in the custom of people at that time, and this is connected to His saying: ﴿and a great kingdom﴾ (Al-Insan: 20).

Nafi', Hamza and Abu Ja'far read ﴿'Aliyahum﴾ with a sukun on the ya' (ʿāliyuhum, "their upper garments"), taking the statement as a new resumptive clause (isti'naf bayani, a clause that answers an implied question) explaining the clause "you would see bliss and a great kingdom." So ﴿'Aliyuhum﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), and ﴿thiyabu sundusin﴾ is its predicate-subject (fa'il) which takes the place of the predicate (sadd masadd al-khabar). It governs its own agent (fa'il) even though it does not depend on a negation, an interrogation or a qualifier. This is the dialect of the Banu Lahab (Khabir), and the clause stands in the position of explanation for the clause ﴿you would see bliss﴾ (Al-Insan: 20).

The rest of the Ten Readers read ﴿'Aliyahum﴾ with a fatha on the ya', taking it as a singular circumstantial qualifier (hal mufrad) for ﴿al-abrar﴾ (the righteous), meaning: that is the condition of the people of great dominion.

The idafa (genitive construction) of ﴿thiyab﴾ to ﴿sundus﴾ is explanatory (bayaniyya), like "a ring of gold" and "a garment of silk," meaning: garments made of it.

Al-sundus is thin brocade (al-dibaj al-raqiq). Al-istabraq is thick brocade (al-dibaj al-ghalidh). Both were discussed under His saying: ﴿and they will wear green garments of sundus and istabraq﴾ (Al-Kahf: 31) in Surat al-Kahf. Both are Arabized words.

As for al-sundus, it is Arabized from the Indian language, and its original form is (sundun) with a nun at the end. It is said that the reason for this naming is that it was brought to Iskandar (Alexander), and he was told that its name was (sundun), so he changed it into the Greek form sundus, because they often give names ending in the letter sin, and the Arabs made it sundus. In al-Lisan it is stated that sundus is made from al-mir'izza (a kind of goat's hair); this is how its editor vocalized it, but the known word is al-mir'iz, as in al-Tadhkira and Shifa' al-Ghalil. In al-Tadhkira: al-mir'iz is what is soft and long of wool. End of quote. Perhaps it is the wool of a particular animal that has length, or it is of the type of hair. The apparent meaning is that it is only green in colour, according to the saying of Yazid ibn Hudhaq al-'Abdi describing his horse's pasture:

"I treated it until it became Abyssinian-coloured, as if upon it were sundus and sudus."

That is, in land of intense greenness, like the colour of the Abyssinian. In al-Lisan: al-sudus is the green tayalisan (a shawl). And according to the saying of Abu Tammam, mourning Muhammad ibn Humayd al-Nabhani al-Tusi:

"Death clothed him in red garments, but the night did not come upon them except that they were of green sundus."

As for al-istabraq, it is a weave of Persian weaving, and its name is Persian; its original form in Persian is istaqrah.

The meaning is that above them are garments of both kinds, they wear this and that, combining the excellences of both, and this is the most splendid clothing of kings and of people of wealth.

The green colour is more pleasing to the eye and was among the emblems of kings. Al-Nabigha said praising the kings of Ghassan:

"They protect bodies whose bliss is ancient, in pure sleeves, with green shoulders."

The apparent meaning is that sundus was not dyed except green.

Nafi' and Hafs read ﴿khudrun﴾ with raf' (khudrun, green) as an attribute of ﴿thiyab﴾ (garments). And ﴿istabraqun﴾ with raf' also, as coordinated with ﴿thiyab﴾ under the condition that they are of sundus; so the meaning of ﴿'aliyuhum istabraq﴾ is that istabraq is their clothing.

Ibn Kathir and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read ﴿khudrin﴾ with jarr (khudrin) as an attribute (na't) of ﴿sundus﴾, and ﴿istabraqun﴾ with raf' coordinated with ﴿thiyab﴾.

Ibn 'Amir, Abu 'Amr, Abu Ja'far and Ya'qub read ﴿khudrun﴾ with raf' and ﴿istabraqin﴾ with jarr, coordinated with ﴿sundusin﴾, with the implied meaning: and garments of istabraq.

Hamza and al-Kisa'i read ﴿khudrin﴾ with jarr as an attribute of ﴿sundus﴾, considering that it explains the garments, so it has the sense of plural. They both read ﴿istabraqin﴾ (Al-Rahman: 54) with jarr, coordinated with sundus.

Al-asawir (bracelets) is the plural of siwar, an ornament whose shape is cylindrical and hollow in the middle, worn by women on their wrists; men do not wear it except kings. The mention of the bracelets of Kisra (Khosrow) occurs in a hadith.

This is a precaution (ihtiras, a safeguard against misunderstanding) against what their drinking from the cup mixed with camphor and ginger might suggest, namely that it might contain what similar drinks contain in this world, such as intoxication (ghawl), foul speech and idle talk. So He expressed this by describing their drink as ṭahūr (pure), in the intensive form of purity, which is freedom from impurities, meaning: free from what is in other drinks of corruption and defilement.

He attributed the giving of drink to their Lord to show their honour, meaning: He Himself commanded that they be given drink, just as it is said: "The master of the house fed them and gave them drink."

This saying is the speech of an omitted "saying," whose indication is the address itself, since nothing preceding this address is suitable for it except that the addressees are the righteous (al-abrar), whose delight is described.

The omitted saying may be estimated as a verb in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun of the absent party in "saqahum" (He gave them to drink), such as: "It is said to them," or "their Lord says to them." The demonstrative "this" refers to what is present before them of the varieties of the delight described in the verses preceding.

The purpose of this is praise of them for what they had advanced of the fear of God, honouring them with it, and cheering their souls by informing them that what has been bestowed upon them is their due, as a recompense for their deeds.

The insertion of the verb (kāna) is like the insertion of its counterpart previously.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 76, verses 23–24:

﴿Indeed, it is We who have sent down the Qur'an to you, in gradual revelation.﴾ ﴿So be patient for the decree of your Lord, and do not obey from among them any sinner or ungrateful one.﴾

From here begins what there is no disagreement is Meccan of this surah.

On both opinions, this is an independent new statement (isti'naf ibtida'i). It fits the view of the majority that the whole surah is Meccan, which is the more preponderant view, as a resumption that shifts from argument for the proof of resurrection, and from warning and threat to the disbelievers in it, and from encouragement and promise to the believers in it, with deterrents and incentives that concern the conditions that will follow resurrection. When that had been fully covered, the course of speech was turned back to the steadying of the Messenger (ﷺ) and the strengthening of his heart, to ward off the afflictions of grief that might reach him because of his people's obstinacy in their disbelief and their denial of what was sent down to him, a matter that tends to weaken human resolve. So God reminded him that He had sent down the Book to him, so that he would not heed their denial.

In placing this after the long discourse on the conditions of the Hereafter, there is a fulfilment of the due attention to the conditions of people in this world. It begins with the condition of the noblest of people, who is the Messenger (ﷺ), then with the condition of those whom the Messenger (ﷺ) invited, between those who (﴿love the fleeting [life]﴾ [al-Insan: 27]) and (﴿whoever takes a way to his Lord﴾ [al-Insan: 29]), and He admitted them into His mercy.

The affirmation of the statement with (inna) is for the sake of giving it importance.

The affirmation of the attached pronoun by a detached pronoun in his saying (﴿Innā naḥnu﴾) serves to establish the meaning of the pronoun, as a verbal emphasis, to draw attention to the greatness of that pronoun, so that it leads to greater concern with the statement, since it is established that it is the act of the one to whom those two pronouns refer, for He does not act except in a deed bound to wisdom and utmost rectitude.

This is from metaphorical kinaya (kinayah ramziyyah). Furthermore, the statement as a whole is used in its necessary meaning, which is steadfastness and support, so the whole of it is a metaphorical kinaya.

The choice of the verb (nazzalna), which indicates its being sent down in stages, verses and surahs, as a gradual revelation (tanzil), is an idmaj (incidental inclusion) that hints that this was part of God's wisdom, which the affirmation with (inna) and the affirmation of the attached pronoun by the detached pronoun point to; thus there is gathered in it an emphasis upon an emphasis, and that

صفحة ٤٠٣
conveys the sense of restriction (qasr), since restriction and specification are nothing but an emphasis upon an emphasis, as al-Sakkaki said. So the meaning is: It is not other than I who sent down the Qur'an to you.

In it there is also an allusion (ta'rid) to the polytheists who said (﴿Why was the Qur'an not sent down to him all at once?﴾ [al-Furqan: 32]), for they made its gradual sending down a pretext for doubt that it is from God.

The meaning is: None sent it down in stages except Me, and My wisdom required that I send it down to you in stages.

Following upon this preparation is His command to him to be patient with the burdens of the message and with what he meets in it of the harm of the polytheists, and to strengthen his resolve so that it does not falter.

He called that a decree (hukm) because the conveying of a message from God leaves the messenger no choice in accepting it and undertaking its affairs, and because what surrounds it of the difficulties of reforming the community and bringing it to what is good for it in this world and the next, and enduring all kinds of harm in the course of that until he completes what God commanded him, is like a judgment upon the Messenger to accept what reaches the limit of endurance until a term fixed with God.

The verb (isbir) is construed with (lam) to imply that patience includes the sense of submission and obedience to a hard command, and it may be construed with (ʿalā), as God said (﴿And be patient over what they say﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 10]). The context of the discourse favours one of the two constructions, as has been explained earlier at His saying (﴿And for your Lord, be patient﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 7]) in Surat al-Muddaththir.

Since among the forms of their turning away from accepting his call is a form in which there are desires on their part, such as that he should cease striking them with the thunderbolts of the revelation, by denigrating their opinion and belittling their religion and their idols, and perhaps they offered him marriage ties with them, or the giving of wealth from them, his command to be patient was followed by patience against what is among the forms of turning away in firmness and severity, by forbidding him to obey them in the other form of turning away, which is couched in gentleness and desire.

In this prohibition there is an emphasis on the command to be patient, since the prohibition against it encompasses everything that removes the requirements of the patience intended here.

The purpose of this prohibition is to make them despair of his granting their requests when he recites this verse to them, because they reckon that what they offered him would turn him away from what he is engaged in of the call, since they are far removed from grasping the reality of the message and the integrity of the Messenger (ﷺ).

صفحة ٤٠٤
Obedience (ta'a) is carrying out a demand by doing what is demanded and by refraining from what is forbidden. The polytheists used to make demands of the Prophet (ﷺ) that he do what they desired, such as driving away the weak among the believers from the assembly, bringing a Qur'an other than this one or altering it to suit their circumstances, and that he refrain from what they did not want to occur, such as belittling their gods and praying aloud. So God warned him against listening to their words and against their hopes of achieving what they desired.

The apparent construction would be: "and do not obey them," or "and do not obey any of them," but he turned away from it to (﴿sinner or ungrateful﴾), to indicate by the two descriptions that their obedience leads to committing sin or disbelief, because in that they usually command him and forbid him, so they only command what suits their qualities.

Thus what is meant by the sinner and the ungrateful is the two categories of those described, and the linking of the forbidden obedience to these two types suggests that the two descriptions are the reason for the prohibition.

The sinner and the ungrateful are mutually entailing, so mentioning one of the two descriptions would suffice without the other, but he combined them to disparage the state of the one characterized by both, as God said (﴿And God does not love every ungrateful sinner﴾ [al-Baqarah: 276]).

In mentioning these two descriptions there is also an allusion to two leaders of disbelief and obstinacy, namely 'Utbah ibn Rabi'ah and al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, for 'Utbah was well known for committing sins and transgressions, and al-Walid was known for his fierce stubbornness in disbelief and arrogance. Both were disbelievers, so each of them is pointed to by that for which he was a byword among the rest of the polytheists: for the first, the abundance of sins, and for the second, the excess in disbelief. For this reason the intensive form (kafur) was applied to him.

It is said that 'Utbah offered the Prophet (ﷺ) that he should give up calling people to Islam and that he would marry him to his daughter, who was among the most beautiful women of Quraysh. And al-Walid offered him wealth that would satisfy him if he gave up the call, and al-Walid was among the wealthiest of Quraysh, and he is the one about whom God said (﴿And I made for him wealth extended﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 12]). So in choosing these two descriptors for mention there is an incidental inclusion (idmaj) for censuring them both and an allusion to their story.

Whatever the case, the particle (aw) has not gone beyond its basic meaning of coordinating the sharing of one of two things, or several things, in a statement or a demand. This sharing conveys choice, permission, division, doubt, or uncertainty, according to its positions and the governing factors of inflection, so that (aw) may be followed by an implied (an), which then puts the imperfect verb in the subjunctive. That the one shared with it is one of several is necessary to all its positions.

Thus the meaning of the verse is a prohibition against obeying either one of these two described persons, and it is understood that obeying both of them is also forbidden by implication, because if he obeys both together, he has certainly obeyed one of them and more.

The position of (min-hum) is that of a circumstantial phrase (hal) relative to (āthiman), for it is a description of (āthiman), and when the description was placed before the described it became a circumstantial phrase.

(Min) is partitive. The pronoun governed by it refers to the polytheists, and no antecedent has preceded for them, because they are known from the context of the call, or because they are what is understood from His saying (﴿Indeed, it is We who have sent down the Qur'an to you﴾), that is, not as the polytheists claim, that you brought it of your own accord, and from His saying (﴿So be patient for the decree of your Lord﴾), that is, patient over the harm of the polytheists.

The meaning is interpreted as: "and do not obey any one of the polytheists."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 76, verses 25–26:

﴿And remember the name of your Lord morning and evening.﴾ ﴿And of the night, prostrate to Him and glorify Him through a long night.﴾

That is: turn your attention to your task of calling to God and remembering God in its various forms. This is guidance toward what helps him to be patient over what they say.

By "morning and evening" is meant the encompassing of the times of the day, that is, that their turning away should not prevent you from repeating and renewing the call at both ends of the day. Remembrance of God includes the prayers, such as His saying: ﴿And establish prayer at the two ends of the day and in the first hours of the night. Indeed, good deeds remove evil deeds. That is a reminder for those who remember.﴾ [Hud: 114] ﴿And be patient, for indeed Allah does not allow the reward of the doers of good to be lost.﴾ [Hud: 115]. Likewise the voluntary acts that are among the particular features of the Prophet ﷺ, both those that are obligatory among them and those that are not obligatory. So the imperative in His saying "and remember" is used in the general sense of demand, encompassing obligation and supererogation.

Mentioning the name of the Lord includes conveying the call, includes worshipping God in the obligatory and voluntary prayers, and includes admonition by warning of His punishment and hoping for His reward.

This verse came in accordance with His, Exalted, saying ﴿And We certainly know that your breast becomes constricted by what they say. So glorify your Lord with praise and be among those who prostrate﴾ [Al-Hijr: 97], and His saying ﴿And remember the name of your Lord and devote yourself to Him with complete devotion﴾ [Al-Muzzammil: 8] ﴿Lord of the east and the west; there is no deity except Him, so take Him as Disposer of affairs﴾ [Al-Muzzammil: 9] ﴿And be patient over what they say﴾ [Al-Muzzammil: 10].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 76, verse 27:

[Page 407]
﴿Indeed, these people love the immediate (transient life) and leave behind them a heavy Day.﴾

This is a reason (ta'lil) for the prohibition in His saying: (﴿And do not obey from among them any sinner or ungrateful one.﴾ [al-Insan: 24]), meaning: because their disposition is absorption in this world together with turning away from the Hereafter, since they do not believe in the Resurrection; so if he (the Prophet) were to obey them, he would take on their disposition. The Exalted said: (﴿They wish that you would disbelieve as they disbelieved, so that you would be equal. So do not take from among them allies﴾ [al-Nisa: 89]), and so on. Thus the position of (inna, "indeed") is that of causal explanation, and it is like the causal fa' (fa' al-sababiyyah), as the Shaykh 'Abd al-Qahir (al-Jurjani) pointed out.

(Ha'ulaa', "these") is a demonstrative referring to people present in the mind of the addressee because of the frequency of speech about them. I have inductively concluded from the Qur'an that when (ha'ulaa') is used without a prior mention of what it refers to, the intended referents are the polytheists. I have mentioned this in my commentary on His saying (﴿So if these disbelieve in it, We have already entrusted it to a people who are not disbelievers in it﴾) in Surat al-An'am, and on His saying (﴿So do not be in doubt about what these worship﴾ [Hud: 109]) in Surat Hud.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was far removed from love of this world, and he said: "What have I to do with the world?" He had no love for its affairs except women and perfume, as he said: "Women and perfume have been made beloved to me from your world."

As for women, inclination toward them is firmly rooted in the natural disposition of males, and what is natural does not fail; and in intimacy with them there is a revival of the soul. So enjoying them is praiseworthy when it occurs in a manner free from falling into corruption. The most excellent enjoyment is like eating food and drinking water. The Exalted said: (﴿And We had certainly sent messengers before you and given them wives and offspring﴾ [al-Ra'd: 38]).

As for perfume, it is because it is suited to purification of the soul.

The present tense in (yuhibbuna, "they love") indicates the recurrence of this, meaning that this is their habit and custom: they do not combine love of the Hereafter with love of the immediate life. "Al-'ajilah" is an adjective of a deleted noun known from context, its estimated form being: al-hayat al-'ajilah ("the immediate life") or al-dar al-'ajilah ("the immediate abode"). What is meant by it is the duration of the life of this world.

The use of "al-'ajilah" for this world is frequent in the Qur'an, such as His saying (﴿Nay, but you love the immediate (life) and leave the Hereafter﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 20]), so calling this world "al-'ajilah" became widespread among Muslims.

[Page 408]
The object of (yuhibbuna) is a deleted genitive construction, its estimated form being: delight or benefits, because love does not attach to the essence of this world itself.

In choosing to mention this world with the attribute "immediate" there is a preparation for the intended blame, because the description "immediate" suggests that they preferred it because it is immediate. In this there is an implicit rebuke of their foolishness, for they were content with the base because it is immediate, and this is not among the traits of people of insight. Therefore His saying (﴿and leave behind them a heavy Day﴾) comes as a completion of the basis of their blame and their being called foolish, for if they loved this world while preparing for the Hereafter, they would not be blameworthy. The Exalted said, recounting the words of the counselors to Qarun: (﴿And seek, through what Allah has given you, the Abode of the Hereafter, and do not forget your share of this world﴾ [al-Qasas: 77]). This is similar to His saying (﴿They know an outward appearance of the worldly life, but they are heedless of the Hereafter﴾ [al-Rum: 7]), since the basis of blame there is that they confined themselves to knowledge of worldly affairs while turning away from knowledge of the Hereafter.

They are depicted as one who leaves something behind him, so he does not strive toward it, but strives toward what is before him.

They turned away from it only because they do not believe in its arrival, so how would they strive toward it?

The present tense in (yadharuna, "they leave") requires that they persist in this, and that this is renewed and recurrent among them; they do not fail in this leaving, because they do not believe in the coming of that Day. As for the Muslims, they do not leave behind them this Day, because they are never free of works for it, with variation among them in piety.

The heavy Day is the Day of Resurrection. It is described as "heavy" by way of metaphor for the severity of the hardships and distresses that occur in it, so it is like a heavy object that cannot be borne.

Heaviness (thiql) is used metaphorically for severity and difficulty. The Exalted said: (﴿Heavy it became in the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-A'raf: 187]) and said: (﴿Indeed, We will cast upon you a heavy word﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 5]).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 76, verse 28:

Page 409
﴿We created them and strengthened their frame, and when We will, We can substitute their likes with a complete substitution.﴾
Since the report about them, that they "leave behind them a heavy day" (﴿They leave behind them a heavy day﴾ [al-Insan: 27]), implies that they deny the occurrence of that day, as we have already mentioned, and since the motive that led them to deny it was the doubt about the impossibility of restoring bodies after they have decayed and perished, and since the preceding speech was driven in the manner of censure of them and rebuke against them, here comes what serves as evidence against their denial and as a refutation of their doubt, by demonstrating the possibility of restoring their creation: the One who created them the first time will bring them back, as He, exalted is He, said (﴿They will say, "Who will restore us?" Say, "The One who originated you the first time."﴾ [al-Isra': 51]), along with other verses revolving around this meaning.

The opening of the sentence with the subject, whose predicate is a verbal predicate, rather than beginning with ﴿We created them﴾ or "We are the Creators," serves to affirm the strength and certainty of the predicate with regard to those addressed by this speech; although it is not addressed to them, they are its intended object.

The strengthening of the ruling is based on treating those created beings as if they were someone who doubts that God created them, since they did not act in accordance with what knowledge requires, so they denied that God restores creation after decay; it is as though they attribute the first creation to someone other than Him. The strengthening of the ruling entails that when He wills, He substitutes their likes by restoring their bodies. Therefore the sentence ﴿and when We will, We can substitute their likes﴾ did not need to be emphasized, being sufficed by the meaning generated from the preceding sentence, although by the rule of apparent sense it was more deserving of emphasis. This strengthening here indicates that a statement following it is the target of the emphasis, and its parallel in emphasis and branching is His saying, exalted is He (﴿We created you, so why do you not believe? Have you considered what you emit?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 57]) up to His saying (﴿And We are not outdone in substituting your likes﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 60]), for the branched element is ﴿Have you considered what you emit?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 58] and what is connected to it. The clause ﴿so why do you not believe?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 57] is a parenthetical insertion, and this has passed in surah al-Waqi'ah.

So "their likes" are the second bodies, since they are likenesses of their bodies that existed at the time of the revelation.

Al-shadd (tightening) is the making firm and perfecting of the connection of the parts of the body with one another through the bones, sinews and veins, for by this the body becomes self-sufficient.

Al-asr (binding) is the tie, and it is used here for firmness and perfection by way of metaphor.

Page 410
The meaning: We made firm the binding of the parts of their bodies, so that they were held fast, some to others.
His saying: ﴿and when We will, We can substitute their likes﴾ is information that God is able to substitute them with other people.

The omission of the object of ﴿We will﴾ is because the answer of (idha, "when") indicates it, as is generally the case with the verb of willing.

The use of (idha) in this conditional is because the nature of (idha) is to convey certainty of the occurrence of what is conditioned by it, unlike the particle (in, "if"); so it is an indication that the occurrence of this will is closely expected.

It is possible that this is in the position of a conclusion to His saying ﴿We created them﴾ etc., and the condition is taken as a certainty. God, exalted is He, said (﴿And indeed the Judgment is surely to occur﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 6]).

It is also possible that His saying ﴿and when We will, We can substitute their likes﴾ is a threat to them for their aversion and their denial of resurrection, meaning: if We willed, We would destroy them and create another creation like them, as in His saying, exalted is He (﴿If He wills, He can take you away and bring a new creation﴾ [Ibrahim: 19]).

And (idha) would be intended to establish the necessary connection between the condition of (idha) and its answer, that is, the clause annexed to it and the clause dependent upon it.

The verb of substitution (tabdil) requires a substituted thing and a substitute, and whichever of the two you take as being in the place of the other is valid, because every thing substituted for something is also the thing for which that thing is substituted; especially when there is no purpose in the context to specify what is desired to be acquired and what is permitted to be given up from the two substituted items. Therefore the complement of (baddalna, "We substituted") was omitted here, namely the genitive introduced by the preposition bi-, since it is more deserving of omission, while the direct object was retained.

A parallel to this has already occurred in surah al-Waqi'ah in His saying (﴿upon Our substituting your likes﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 61]), and among it is His saying, exalted is He (﴿Indeed We are able to substitute better than them﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 40]) in surah al-Ma'arij. The estimated sense is: We substituted from them.

Al-amthal (likes) is the plural of mithl, which is that which is similar in essence or attribute. So it is possible that what is meant by "their likes" is their likenesses in the forms of their bodies, and this is the substitution that will take place in the Return.

Page 411
It is also possible that what is meant by "their likes" is that they are nations. On the first aspect, it indicates that resurrection takes place through the creation of bodies in the likeness of the bodies that were in the present life, for the spirits that were in them.
The word (tabdilan, "a substitution") is in the accusative as an absolute object emphasizing its verb, to indicate that it is a true substitution, and in order to reach, through the tanwin, its magnification and wonderment.

This is an initial resumptive sentence (isti'naf ibtida'i), marking a transition from the extended presentation of admonition and argument to a summation of the purpose of the surah and its conclusion. It signals that the intended aim has been completed, draws attention to its benefit and the way one may profit from it, urges reflection upon it, and calls for deriving its fruit. In view of what branches from this sentence, namely His saying ﴿so whoever wills takes a way to his Lord﴾ and so on, the position of the summation for the sentence is strengthened, and the emphasis of the statement by the particle (inna) is because the condition of the addressees is their lack of concern for it, for they deny that it is a reminder.

The reference is to the preceding verses, or to the surah, and for this reason the feminine demonstrative noun was used.

Al-tadhkira (reminder) is a verbal noun of dhakkarahu, like al-tazkiya. That is, I speak to him with words that remind him of what he may have forgotten. It is applied here to exhortation to abandon an evil deed and turn toward a righteous deed, and to the clarity of good and evil for one who takes heed, that is, one who becomes perceptive. This is by way of comparing the state of one who turns away from good and is preoccupied with other things to the state of one who has forgotten it, because it is his nature not to neglect it except one who has forgotten its benefit to him.

Following this is the exhortation to take the path of seeking the pleasure of God, by His saying ﴿so whoever wills takes a way to his Lord﴾, meaning: after this reminder there is nothing but acting upon it, if the one who is reminded wills to act upon it.

In His saying (whoever wills) there is an exhortation to hasten to this, because a person's will is within his capacity, and nothing prevents him from it except poor management of his affairs.

This is an exhortation and incitement, containing an allusion to the polytheists, that they refused to take heed out of obstinacy and envy.

Taking a path (ittikhadh al-sabil) means following it. The following is expressed by "taking" by way of metaphor, through the comparison

[Page 412]

So in His saying ﴿took a way to his Lord﴾ there are two metaphors, because "the way" is used metaphorically for the means of attaining success with bliss and nearness.
His saying ﴿to his Lord﴾ is connected to "a way", meaning a way that conveys one to God. Rational people do not differ regarding the nobility of what leads to the Lord, that is, to His honour, because that is the abode of all goods. For this reason "Lord" is expressed in the form of a noun in annexation to the pronoun of "whoever wills", since the happiness of the servant lies in being favoured with his Lord.

This way is repentance. The penitent is like one who was astray or a runaway slave who found the road by which he returns to his destination, or one who travelled the road to his master.

The parallel of this verse has already been mentioned in the surah al-Muzzammil.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 76, verse 30:

﴿And you do not will except that Allah wills. Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing, Wise.﴾

When He attached their choice of the path to the pleasure of Allah to their own will, He followed it with a reminder to turn toward seeking the pleasure of Allah, so that by means of His good pleasure they might gain facility in following the paths of goodness. For when they stand in a place of divine pleasure and care, He shows them kindness and makes easy for them what is hard for souls: patience in abandoning the destructive desires. He said (﴿So We will ease him toward ease﴾ [al-Layl: 7]). But if they do not strive toward the pleasure of their Lord, He leaves them to the states to which they have become accustomed, and these carry them into the deserts of blindness, since they are surrounded by causes of misdirection through what their natural dispositions have settled upon: preferring desires and rushing headlong with the bands of errors. This is what His words convey (﴿So We will ease him toward hardship﴾ [al-Layl: 10]), meaning We leave him to himself, so that hardship becomes easy for him, that is, it reaches him without effort or struggle.

The clause (﴿And you do not will except that Allah wills﴾) may be a continuation of the clause (﴿Whoever wills takes to his Lord a way﴾ [al-Insan: 29]), or a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from (man yashā᾽) [whoever]. In both cases it is a completion (tatmīm) and a safeguard (iḥtirās).

The object of tashā᾽ūna (you will) is omitted to indicate generality, and the implied meaning is: "and you do not will anything, or any willing," and the generality of persons entails the generality of states and times, that is, you do not will anything at any time or in any state.

The connection between the occurrence of their will and the will of Allah is explained by the fact that Allah is Knowing and Wise: Knowing of the means by which the good of their will is brought into existence, and Wise regarding the subtleties of that, which human minds cannot fully reach in their essence, because there are exalted operations whose details people cannot fully comprehend. Rather, it is enough for them to be guided by their effects and to purify their souls so as to turn away from neglecting reflection upon them.

Here "mā" is negating, and the exception is from the generality of things willed, their states and their times. Since what follows the exception particle is a particle of the verbal noun (ḥarf maṣdar), it is determined that the excepted element is to be taken as a verbal noun: "except the willing of Allah," that is, His willing. It is suitable for considering the verbal noun sense, for considering the state, and for considering the time, because the verbal noun is able to denote all three according to the interpretation. If a noun is supplied (muḍāf), the meaning is: "except in the state of Allah's willing" or "except in the time of His willing." If no noun is supplied, the meaning is: "You have no will in reality except following the will of Allah."

The choice of the verbal particle "an" (that) is part of the inimitability of the Qur'an.

It is also possible that both verbs, tashā᾽ūna and (yashā᾽ Allāh), are treated as intransitive, so that no objects are supplied for them, following the manner of al-Buhturi's saying:

"That a seer sees and a hearer hears."

And the exception may be from states, that is: "you do not have your will come about in any state except in the state of the coming about of Allah's will." In all of this there is an indication of the subtlety of the reality of the servant's will in relation to the will of Allah, and this is the meaning which al-Ash'ari gathered under the term kasb (acquisition). It has been said of it: "More subtle than the acquisition of al-Ash'ari." So in the verse there is an alert to people to this hidden meaning, so that they may observe it in themselves and find its signs present and abundant. For this reason the description of this will is elaborated by the concluding phrase (﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing, Wise﴾), which is either a concluding remark (tadhyīl) or a causal clause (ta'līl) for the clause (﴿He admits whom He wills into His mercy﴾ [al-Insan: 31]), that is: because it is necessary for Him to have knowledge and wisdom, He is most knowing. So whoever He wills to admit into His mercy, He admits, and whoever He wills to keep far from it, He keeps far.

This elaboration has no parallel in His words in Surah 'Abasa (﴿No indeed, this is a reminder; so whoever wills, let him remember it﴾), because attaining remembrance from a reminder is closer and more attainable than acting upon it, which is expressed by the path leading to Allah. Therefore the attention and concern are directed toward what hints at the means of taking that path.

The verb (kāna, was/is) indicates that His description with knowledge and wisdom is an essential attribute, because both are necessary for Him.

From the beginning and the end of this verse there results the establishment of two wills: one is the will of the servants, and the other is the will of Allah. This verse gathers them both, and so it became a foundation for reconciling the apparently conflicting Qur'anic verses, some of which, taken alone, attach the duties, their rewards and punishments to the will of the servants regarding the actions they willed for themselves, while others attach a will to Allah regarding the actions of His servants.

As for the will of the servants, when it arises, it comes about directly through the affectedness of souls by the agency of encouragement and warning. As for the will of Allah, by the affectedness of souls is meant the effects of the divine will, which, if they come about, then the will of the servant comes about, and we know that Allah willed that for His servant. Those effects are a totality of matters that converge and gather, and from them the will of the servant arises.

Those effects are what exists in the order of the world and of humankind from the effects of Allah's power and creation: the influence of time and place, the formation of creation, the composition of the body and the mind, the extent of the capacity for understanding and comprehension, the domination of society, environment, propaganda and indoctrination over all of that, together with what in all of it is correct or mistaken. When the causes for accepting guidance are established from the totality of those effects, and some of them harmonize with others, or their good outweighs their evil, we recognize the will of Allah, because those are the effects of His will within the total order of the world, and because He, exalted, knows that they will be established for a particular person. So His knowledge of their abundance, given that they are effects of His order in creation, is what is meant by His will. And when they are reversed and some of them clash with others, and their good does not prevail over their evil, but rather their evil prevails over their good with respect to an individual person, the arrival of good to his soul is frustrated, and so he did not will it. We then know that Allah did not will for him the acceptance of good, and we know that Allah knows what surrounds that individual. This is the meaning of Allah not willing good for him, or, in other words, that He willed for him to will evil. There is no escape for the servant from this noose except when a care from Allah and a kindness turn toward him, and He creates existents which, when they enter into what surrounds the servant of causes and states, change their states and reverse their effects, so that the servant moves to righteousness after having been immersed in corruption. A new state is thereby made ready for the servant, contrary to what surrounded him, just as happened to 'Umar ibn al-Khattab in accepting great guidance and advancing far into it, at a time when he was clothed in thorough misguidance and obstinacy.

Such a thing is an honor from Allah to the servant and a care for him, and this care arises only by a specific will of Allah: either because His wisdom required it, to bring people out of evil into good, as the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "O Allah, strengthen Islam with one of the two 'Umars," or by answering the supplication of one who prayed and was answered. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab embraced Islam following the aforementioned supplication of the Prophet ﷺ, and he entered Islam following the Prophet's ﷺ saying to him: "Has the time not come for you, O son of al-Khattab, to submit?" Do you not see that the great guidance bestowed upon Muhammad ﷺ was a result of the supplication of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, in his words (﴿Our Lord, and send among them a messenger from themselves﴾ [al-Baqarah: 129]), the verse. The Prophet ﷺ said: "I am the answer to the supplication of Ibrahim."

This is what could be explained of these two wills to the extent possible. Perhaps in this there is what clarifies the saying of Shaykh Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari regarding the meaning of kasb and istita'ah (capacity): that it is the soundness of causes and instruments.

By this the doctrine of the Jabriyya (determinists) is refuted, because the verse establishes a will for people and makes the will of Allah a condition for it, since the exception is in the force of a condition. So the human being has his will without doubt.

As for the doctrine of the Mu'tazila, it is not far from the saying of al-Ash'ari, except in the expression "creation" or "acquisition," and al-Ash'ari's expression is more elegant and more closely bound to proper courtesy toward Allah the Creator, and except in establishing the meaning of the will of Allah and the distinction between it and command, or the absence of distinction, and its detailed treatment belongs in the science of kalam.

Nafi', 'Asim, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Ya'qub read (﴿wa-mā tashā᾽ūna﴾) with the second-person ta' of address, as a shift (iltifat) from the third person to the second person. Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, Abu 'Amr and Khalaf read it with the third-person ya', referring back to (man shā᾽a) [whoever].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 76, verse 31:

Page 416
﴿He admits whom He wills into His mercy, while for the wrongdoers He has prepared a painful punishment.﴾
It is permissible for this sentence to be resumed (mustaʼnafah) as a clarificatory resumption (istiʼnaf bayani) arising from the sentence ﴿And you do not will except that Allah wills﴾ [al-Insan: 30]. The listener, following the mention of the will of Allah, wonders about the case of ﴿whoever takes a way to his Lord﴾ [al-Insan: 29] and whoever does not take a way to Him. So it is answered that He admits into His mercy whoever He wills to take a way to Him, and that He has prepared for whoever does not take a way to Him a painful punishment, and those are the wrongdoers.

It is also permissible for this sentence to be the predicate (khabar) of inna (indeed) in the phrase ﴿Indeed Allah﴾, and the sentence ﴿was Knowing, Wise﴾ [al-Insan: 30] would then be a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraD) between the subject of inna and its predicate, or a circumstantial clause (hal). In both cases it indicates that the attribution of the two descriptors, the All-Knowing and the All-Wise, to the Name of Majesty (Allah) is meant to alert that all His acts, whether a recompense of mercy or of punishment, proceed according to His knowledge and wisdom.

The word ﴿the wrongdoers﴾ (al-zalimin) is in the accusative because it is the object of a verb omitted, indicated by what is mentioned, by way of the rule of ishtighal (occupation of the noun by a verb). The estimate is: "He threatens the wrongdoers," or "He requites," or something similar, of what the listener judges suitable to the verb mentioned after it.

Surah al-Mursalat

It has no explicit naming from the Prophet (ﷺ) by which the word "surah" is added to its first sentence.

It was named during the era of the Companions as the surah of ﴿By those sent forth in gusts﴾ [al-Mursalat: 1]. In the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud in the two Sahihs: "While we were with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in a cave at Mina, there was revealed to him the surah of ﴿By those sent forth in gusts﴾ [al-Mursalat: 1]. He was reciting it, and I was receiving it from his mouth, and his mouth was moist with it, when a snake came out at us..." the hadith.

In the Sahih, from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "I recited the surah of ﴿By those sent forth in gusts﴾ [al-Mursalat: 1], and Umm al-Fadl, the wife of al-'Abbas, heard me and wept, and said: 'My son, you reminded me by your recitation of this surah; it is the last thing I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recite in the Maghrib prayer.'"

It was named "Surah al-Mursalat." Abu Dawud narrated from Ibn Mas'ud: "The Prophet (ﷺ) used to recite the pairs of similar surahs in one rak'ah: al-Rahman and al-Najm in one rak'ah, iqtarabat and al-Haqqah in one rak'ah," then he said, "and ʻamma yatasa'alun and al-Mursalat in one rak'ah." So he made these words a substitute for his saying "the two surahs," and named it al-Mursalat without the waw of oath, because the waw in his speech is the waw of conjunction, like its sisters in his speech.

It became well known in the mushafs by the name "al-Mursalat," and likewise in the tafsirs and in Sahih al-Bukhari.

Al-Khafaji and Sa'd Allah, known as Sa'di, mentioned in their two glosses on al-Baydawi that it is called "Surah al-'Urf," but they gave no chain for it, and the author of al-Itqan did not mention it among the surahs having more than one name.

In al-Itqan, from the Book of Ibn al-Daris, from Ibn 'Abbas, in counting the surahs revealed at Mecca, he mentioned it under the name "al-Mursalat." And in it, from the Dala'il al-Nubuwwah of al-Bayhaqi, from 'Ikrimah and al-Hasan, in counting the surahs revealed at Mecca, he mentioned it under the name "al-Mursalat."

It is Meccan according to the majority of the early exegetes, and this is the apparent meaning of the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud mentioned above, which implies that it is among the earliest surahs of the Qur'an in revelation, since it was revealed while the Prophet (ﷺ) was hiding in a cave at Mina with some of his Companions.

From Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah: the verse ﴿And when it is said to them, bow down, they do not bow down﴾ [al-Mursalat: 48] is Madani, revealed concerning the hypocrites. The reasoning behind that is an interpretation from the one who narrated it from him, in view of the fact that the open disbelievers are not commanded to pray. There is no proof in this that the verse is Madani, for the pronoun in His saying ﴿And when it is said to them﴾ [al-Mursalat: 48] follows the manner of the pronouns before it, all of which refer to the disbelievers, who are the polytheists. The meaning of ﴿it is said to them, bow down﴾ [al-Mursalat: 48] is a metonymy for being told to submit (Islam). Its parallel is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and they were being called to prostration while they were sound﴾ [al-Qalam: 43], so it refers to the polytheists, and His saying ﴿They said: We were not of those who prayed﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 43] up to His saying ﴿and we used to deny the Day of Recompense﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 46].

From Muqatil: "The verse ﴿And when it is said to them, bow down, they do not bow down﴾ [al-Mursalat: 48] was revealed concerning the delegation of Thaqif when they embraced Islam after the battle of Hawazin and came to Medina. The Prophet (ﷺ) commanded them to pray, and they said: 'We will not bend, for it is a reproach upon us.' He said to them: 'There is no good in a religion that has no bowing and prostration.'"

It is the thirty-third surah in the order of revelation according to Jabir ibn Zayd.

Its purposes
It includes an argument for the occurrence of resurrection after the end of this world, and a description of some of the signs of that.

And an argument for the possibility of the re-creation, from what preceded of the creation of man and the creation of the earth.

And a warning to its deniers of the punishment of the Hereafter and a description of its terrors.

And an allusion to a punishment for them in this world, as distinct peoples who denied before them were uprooted, and the contrasting of that with the recompense of honour for the believers.

And a renewed call to Islam and to affirmation of the Qur'an, because its proofs are manifest.
